questions.scenario: You hover in a spaceship just outside a black hole for a while, then return to a friend who stayed far away in deep space.
questions.question: When you compare clocks, whose has ticked less?
questions.explanation: Gravity slows time: the deeper you sit in a gravitational field, the slower your clock runs compared with one far away. Near a black hole the effect can be enormous, so an hour for you could be years for your friend. You'd notice nothing odd while it happened; your own clock always seems normal to you. The difference shows only when you compare.
questions.intuitionTrap: Time feels universal, the same for everyone everywhere.
questions.principle: Gravitational time dilation: clocks deeper in a gravitational field tick more slowly relative to distant clocks.
questions.funFact: Even on Earth it's measurable: atomic clocks a few dozen centimetres higher up run measurably faster.
questions.source: Standard introductory astronomy (e.g. OpenStax Astronomy 2e); NASA
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: Imagine the Sun were instantly replaced by a black hole with exactly the same mass.
questions.question: What would happen to Earth's orbit?
questions.reveal: Nothing; the orbit stays the same.
questions.explanation: From a distance, gravity depends only on mass and distance, not on what the object is made of or how compact it is. A black hole with the Sun's mass would be only about 6 km across, but at Earth's distance its pull would be identical. Earth would keep orbiting exactly as before, though in freezing darkness. Black holes only behave dramatically when you get very close.
questions.intuitionTrap: Black holes are imagined as cosmic vacuum cleaners that suck in everything around them.
questions.principle: Outside a spherical mass, its gravity depends only on its total mass and your distance.
questions.funFact: If Earth were squeezed into a black hole, it would be about the size of a marble.
questions.source: Standard introductory astronomy (e.g. OpenStax Astronomy 2e); NASA
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: Almost every distant galaxy is moving away from us, and the farther away it is, the faster it recedes.
questions.question: Does that mean we're at the centre of the universe?
options: No, every galaxy sees the same
Probably, but we can't be sure
questions.reveal: No; observers in every galaxy would see the same thing.
questions.explanation: Picture raisins in a rising loaf of bread. As the dough expands, every raisin sees all the others moving away, with more distant raisins receding faster, and no raisin is special. Space itself is expanding in the same way, so observers in any galaxy would see the same pattern. A uniform expansion has no centre.
questions.intuitionTrap: If everything moves away from you, you feel like the origin of the motion.
questions.principle: In a uniformly expanding universe, every observer sees recession speed proportional to distance (Hubble's law).
questions.funFact: Not every galaxy is receding: the Andromeda galaxy is heading toward us and should merge with the Milky Way in a few billion years.
questions.source: Standard introductory astronomy (e.g. OpenStax Astronomy 2e); NASA
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: We always see the same face of the Moon. The side we never see is often called the 'dark side'.
questions.question: Is that side permanently dark?
options: No, it gets as much light
It's dark for half the year
questions.reveal: No; it gets just as much sunlight.
questions.explanation: The Moon spins once on its axis in exactly the time it takes to orbit Earth, so the same face always points toward us. But it still turns relative to the Sun, so every part of it gets roughly two weeks of daylight and two weeks of night. When we see a 'new moon', the far side is in full sunshine. It's the far side, not the dark side.
questions.intuitionTrap: 'Never seen by us' gets mixed up with 'never lit'.
questions.principle: Tidal locking synchronises the Moon's rotation with its orbit, which doesn't stop the Sun lighting every side.
questions.funFact: Nobody saw the far side until a Soviet probe photographed it in 1959.
questions.source: Standard introductory astronomy (e.g. OpenStax Astronomy 2e); NASA
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: Shrink the Sun to the size of a grapefruit sitting in your city. Earth becomes a grain of sand about 15 metres away.
questions.question: On that scale, how far away is the nearest other star?
questions.reveal: On another continent, about 4,000 km away.
questions.explanation: At this scale, 1 km of model represents about 10 million km of real space. Proxima Centauri is about 4.2 light-years away, roughly 40 trillion km, which becomes about 4,000 km: another grapefruit-sized star on another continent. In between there's almost nothing. Space is mostly empty on a scale that's hard to picture.
questions.intuitionTrap: Star maps and space art squeeze stars close together.
questions.principle: Interstellar distances are hundreds of thousands of times larger than the distance from Earth to the Sun.
questions.funFact: Voyager 1, our fastest-receding probe, would need tens of thousands of years to travel that far.
questions.source: Standard introductory astronomy (e.g. OpenStax Astronomy 2e); NASA
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: Astronauts float freely inside the International Space Station, about 400 km above Earth.
questions.question: How strong is Earth's gravity at that height, compared with the ground?
questions.explanation: At 400 km up you're only about 6% farther from Earth's centre than at the surface, so gravity is still roughly 90% as strong. Astronauts float because they're in free fall: the station and everything in it are constantly falling toward Earth, but moving sideways so fast, about 7.7 km per second, that they keep missing it. Everything falls together, so nothing presses on the floor.
questions.intuitionTrap: 'Weightless' sounds like 'no gravity'.
questions.principle: Orbiting objects are in continuous free fall; weightlessness comes from falling together, not from absent gravity.
questions.funFact: The ISS circles Earth about every 90 minutes, so its crew see about 16 sunrises a day.
questions.source: Standard introductory astronomy (e.g. OpenStax Astronomy 2e); NASA
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: NASA rovers have photographed sunsets on Mars, where the daytime sky is a dusty butterscotch colour.
questions.question: What colour is the sky around the setting Sun on Mars?
questions.explanation: Mars's thin air is full of fine dust. Those dust grains scatter red light broadly across the sky, giving the daytime butterscotch colour, but they scatter blue light mostly forward, in nearly the same direction the sunlight is travelling. At sunset you're looking along a long dusty path toward the Sun, so a blue glow gathers around it.
questions.intuitionTrap: We expect sunsets to be red everywhere because they are on Earth.
questions.principle: The colour of scattered light depends on the size of the scattering particles and the viewing angle.
questions.funFact: On Earth, sunsets turn red because air molecules scatter blue light out of the long path, leaving the reds.
questions.source: NASA Curiosity and Spirit rover imagery
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: Suppose the Moon disappeared overnight.
questions.question: What would happen to Earth's ocean tides?
questions.explanation: The Sun raises tides too. It's about 27 million times more massive than the Moon but also about 390 times farther away, and tidal force weakens with the cube of distance. The result is that the Sun's tidal effect is roughly 46% of the Moon's. Without the Moon we'd still have two high and two low tides a day, just much smaller, and no cycle of spring and neap tides.
questions.intuitionTrap: Tides are so strongly linked with the Moon that we forget the Sun pulls on the oceans too.
questions.principle: Tidal force depends on mass divided by distance cubed.
questions.funFact: The biggest 'spring' tides happen when the Sun and Moon line up, at new and full moon.

goDeeper.text: Sun: 333,000 Earth masses at 1 AU. Moon: 0.0123 Earth masses at 0.00257 AU. The ratio comes out near 0.46.

questions.source: Standard introductory astronomy (e.g. OpenStax Astronomy 2e); NASA
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: You're in a spacecraft orbiting Earth, a few kilometres behind a space station in the same orbit. You want to catch up with it.
questions.question: Which way should you fire your thruster first?
questions.explanation: Firing forward adds energy and lifts you into a higher orbit, and higher orbits take longer to go around, so you'd drift farther behind. The counterintuitive move is to slow down. You drop into a lower, faster orbit, gain on the station, then fire forward at the right moment to rise back to its altitude. Orbital mechanics often runs opposite to driving instincts.
questions.intuitionTrap: On a road, to catch someone ahead you simply go faster.
questions.principle: Lower orbits have shorter periods; changing speed in orbit changes altitude.
questions.funFact: In 1965 the Gemini 4 crew tried to fly up to their spent rocket stage by thrusting toward it, and kept drifting away.
questions.source: Standard introductory astronomy (e.g. OpenStax Astronomy 2e); NASA
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: Earth's orbit isn't a perfect circle, so its distance from the Sun changes a little during the year.
questions.question: When is Earth closest to the Sun?
questions.reveal: Early January, in the Northern Hemisphere's winter.
questions.explanation: Earth reaches its closest point to the Sun around 3–4 January. Seasons aren't caused by distance, which changes by only about 3%. They're caused by Earth's 23.4° axial tilt, which changes how high the Sun climbs in the sky and how long the days last. In January the Northern Hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun, so it's winter there despite being slightly closer.
questions.intuitionTrap: Closer to a fire is warmer, so summer seems like it must be when we're closest.
questions.principle: Seasons are caused by axial tilt, not by changes in Earth–Sun distance.
questions.funFact: Because of that slight closeness, Earth moves a little faster in its orbit in January, and northern winter is a few days shorter than northern summer.
questions.source: Standard introductory astronomy (e.g. OpenStax Astronomy 2e); NASA
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: A bright shooting star streaks across the night sky.
questions.question: How big is the object making that streak, typically?
questions.reveal: About the size of a grain of sand.
questions.explanation: Most meteors come from specks of comet or asteroid dust, often no bigger than a grain of sand. They slam into the upper atmosphere at tens of kilometres per second, so even a tiny speck carries a lot of energy. It heats and vaporises the grain and makes the air around it glow, creating a streak visible from far away. A shooting star is not a star at all.
questions.intuitionTrap: A streak visible across a huge stretch of sky seems like it must come from something large.
questions.principle: Kinetic energy grows with the square of speed, so tiny high-speed particles can produce bright meteors.
questions.funFact: Earth sweeps up tens of tonnes of this dust every day.
questions.source: Standard introductory astronomy (e.g. OpenStax Astronomy 2e); NASA
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: On a clear night, stars twinkle but the bright planets shine with a much steadier light.
questions.question: Why the difference?
options: Air blurs points, not tiny disks
questions.reveal: Turbulent air scrambles points of light, but planets are tiny disks.
questions.explanation: Pockets of air at different temperatures bend light slightly differently, and they're constantly moving. A star is so far away it's effectively a single point, so its light gets shoved around as a whole and its brightness flickers. A planet is close enough to appear as a tiny disk; each part of the disk twinkles independently, and the flickers average out into a steadier glow.
questions.intuitionTrap: Twinkling looks like a property of the star itself.
questions.principle: Atmospheric turbulence distorts light from point sources more than from extended ones.
questions.funFact: Astronauts above the atmosphere see stars as steady points of light that don't twinkle at all.
questions.source: Standard introductory astronomy (e.g. OpenStax Astronomy 2e); NASA
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: In about 5 billion years, the Sun will run low on hydrogen fuel in its core.
questions.question: How will the Sun end its life?
options: It will explode as a supernova
It will become a black hole
It will end as a white dwarf
questions.reveal: As a white dwarf, without exploding.
questions.explanation: Only stars born with at least about eight times the Sun's mass end in a core-collapse supernova. The Sun will instead swell into a red giant, gently puff its outer layers into space as a glowing shell called a planetary nebula, and leave behind its hot core: a white dwarf about the size of Earth, which slowly cools over billions of years.
questions.intuitionTrap: Supernovae get the headlines, so it seems like every star dies that way.
questions.principle: A star's mass determines its fate: low- and medium-mass stars become white dwarfs.
questions.funFact: A teaspoon of white-dwarf material would weigh several tonnes on Earth.
questions.source: Standard introductory astronomy (e.g. OpenStax Astronomy 2e); NASA
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: Imagine the Sun suddenly vanished.
questions.question: What would Earth do during the first few minutes?
options: Fly off in a straight line at once
Fall toward where the Sun was
questions.reveal: Keep orbiting the empty spot for about 8 minutes.
questions.explanation: Changes in gravity travel at the speed of light. That was confirmed in 2017, when gravitational waves and light from a neutron-star collision arrived within two seconds of each other after a 130-million-year journey. The Sun is about 8 minutes 20 seconds away at light speed, so for that long Earth would keep curving around the empty spot, and sunlight would keep arriving too. Only then would Earth carry on in a straight line.
questions.intuitionTrap: Gravity feels instant, like an invisible rope that would snap immediately.
questions.principle: Changes in a gravitational field propagate at the speed of light.
questions.funFact: For those eight minutes nobody on Earth could tell anything had happened.
questions.caveat: It's a thought experiment: mass can't actually vanish, but the finite speed of gravity is real.
questions.source: Standard introductory astronomy (e.g. OpenStax Astronomy 2e); NASA
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: You watch the Sun set over a flat sea. Its bottom edge just touches the horizon.
questions.question: Where is the Sun really at that moment?
questions.reveal: Already just below the horizon, geometrically.
questions.explanation: Light's 8-minute trip doesn't shift the Sun's place in our sky much: the Sun barely moves in that time, and Earth's spin changes where your horizon is now, not where the light came from. The big effect is our atmosphere. Near the horizon it bends sunlight by about half a degree, roughly the Sun's own width. So when the bottom edge appears to touch the horizon, the whole Sun is geometrically already just below it.
questions.intuitionTrap: 'We see old light' gets misapplied to the Sun's position in the sky.
questions.principle: Atmospheric refraction raises the apparent position of objects near the horizon by about 0.5°.
questions.funFact: Refraction also squashes the setting Sun into an oval, because its lower edge is lifted more than its upper edge.
questions.source: Standard introductory astronomy (e.g. OpenStax Astronomy 2e); NASA
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: Mercury is the planet closest to the Sun. Venus is almost twice as far out.
questions.question: Which planet has the hotter surface?
questions.explanation: Venus has a crushing atmosphere of mostly carbon dioxide, about 90 times the pressure of Earth's, topped with sulfuric-acid clouds. Sunlight that gets through warms the surface, and the thick CO₂ traps the infrared heat trying to escape. The result is around 465 °C everywhere, day and night, hotter than the sunlit side of Mercury, which has almost no atmosphere and plunges to far below freezing at night.
questions.intuitionTrap: Closer to the Sun simply seems hotter.
questions.principle: A thick greenhouse atmosphere can matter more for surface temperature than distance from the star.
questions.funFact: Soviet Venera landers survived on Venus's surface for only about an hour or two before the heat and pressure destroyed them.
questions.source: Standard introductory astronomy (e.g. OpenStax Astronomy 2e); NASA
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: You catch a common cold, which is caused by a virus.
questions.question: Will antibiotics help you get better faster?
questions.explanation: Antibiotics attack structures and processes that bacteria have and our cells don't, such as bacterial cell walls and bacterial ribosomes. Viruses have none of these: they hijack the machinery inside your own cells. So antibiotics have nothing to target. Taking them anyway brings side effects and helps breed antibiotic-resistant bacteria, which is a growing global problem.
questions.intuitionTrap: 'Germs' feel like one category, so one kind of medicine should work on all of them.
questions.principle: Antibiotics target bacteria; viruses replicate inside host cells and are unaffected.
questions.funFact: Alexander Fleming warned in his 1945 Nobel lecture that misusing penicillin could breed resistant bacteria.
questions.caveat: Doctors sometimes do prescribe antibiotics when a bacterial infection develops on top of a viral one.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: Your body is home to trillions of bacteria, most of them in your gut.
questions.question: How does their number compare with the number of human cells in your body?
questions.explanation: A widely quoted claim says bacteria outnumber human cells ten to one, but it traces back to a rough 1970s estimate. A careful 2016 recount put a typical adult at about 30 trillion human cells (mostly red blood cells) and about 38 trillion bacteria. That's roughly one to one. Because bacteria are tiny, they add up to only around 0.2 kg of your body weight.
questions.intuitionTrap: A memorable statistic repeated often enough starts to feel like established fact.
questions.principle: Estimates are only as good as their assumptions; recounting with better data can overturn famous numbers.
questions.funFact: A single bowel movement can shift the ratio noticeably, since it removes a sizeable fraction of gut bacteria.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: Some brain operations are done with the patient awake and talking, after the scalp has been numbed.
questions.question: Does cutting into the brain tissue itself hurt?
questions.explanation: Your brain processes every pain signal in your body, but brain tissue itself has no pain receptors. The scalp, skull lining and blood vessels around the brain do, which is why they're numbed and why headaches can hurt so much. Once the surgeon is through those layers, the brain can be touched without pain, so the patient can stay awake and help the team avoid areas that control speech or movement.
questions.intuitionTrap: The organ that feels all pain seems like it must be able to feel its own.
questions.principle: Pain requires nociceptors; brain tissue has none, though the surrounding membranes do.
questions.funFact: Musicians have played instruments during awake brain surgery so surgeons can protect the regions they need.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: Two parents both have brown eyes.
questions.question: Could they have a blue-eyed child?
questions.explanation: Eye colour is shaped by several genes, mainly variants in and around OCA2 and HERC2. Brown-eyed parents can each carry variants for lighter eyes without showing them. A child who inherits the 'light' combination from both can have blue eyes. It's the classic hidden-trait pattern, even though the real genetics is more complicated than a single gene.
questions.intuitionTrap: Children seem like they should be a blend of what their parents visibly show.
questions.principle: Traits can skip a generation because hidden (recessive) variants can be carried without being expressed.
questions.funFact: All blue-eyed people may share one ancestral variant near the OCA2 gene that arose roughly 6,000–10,000 years ago.
questions.caveat: The old classroom rule that two blue-eyed parents can't have a brown-eyed child isn't absolute either: it's rare, but it happens.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: Someone loses 10 kg of body fat by eating less and moving more.
questions.question: Where did most of that fat's mass actually go?
questions.reveal: Most of it was breathed out as carbon dioxide.
questions.explanation: When fat is burned, its carbon, hydrogen and oxygen atoms end up in carbon dioxide and water. Tracing the atoms shows about 84% of the fat's mass leaves as CO₂ through your lungs, and the rest as water in urine, sweat and breath. The energy is released, but almost no mass turns into energy: chemical reactions convert only a vanishingly small fraction of mass.
questions.intuitionTrap: We talk about 'burning off' fat as if it turns into heat or energy.
questions.principle: Matter is conserved in metabolism; the atoms of oxidised fat leave mainly as exhaled CO₂.
questions.funFact: Every breath out carries away a few milligrams of carbon that was once part of your body.
questions.source: Meerman & Brown (2014), BMJ, 'When somebody loses weight, where does the fat go?'
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: You come down with the flu and your temperature rises to 39 °C, even though you feel cold and shivery.
questions.question: What's going on with your body's thermostat?
questions.reveal: Your brain deliberately raised its target temperature.
questions.explanation: Immune signals tell the hypothalamus, your brain's thermostat, to raise its set point. Your body then works to reach the new target: you shiver and feel cold while heating up, even though you're already above normal. When the fever breaks, the set point drops and you sweat to shed the extra heat. A moderate fever is a regulated response that seems to help fight infection.
questions.intuitionTrap: A fever looks like a malfunction, a system pushed out of control.
questions.principle: Fever is a regulated rise in the hypothalamic temperature set point, triggered by immune signalling molecules.
questions.funFact: Cold-blooded lizards create a 'behavioural fever' when infected, moving to warmer spots to raise their body temperature.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: A freshwater fish is accidentally moved into a tank of seawater.
questions.question: Which way does water move across its cell membranes?
questions.explanation: Osmosis moves water across membranes toward the side with more dissolved particles. Seawater is about three times saltier than a fish's body fluids, so water drains out through its gills and cells. A freshwater fish is built for the opposite problem, water constantly seeping in, which it gets rid of as dilute urine. In seawater it dehydrates while surrounded by water.
questions.intuitionTrap: A fish surrounded by water seems like it can't possibly dry out.
questions.principle: Water moves by osmosis from lower to higher solute concentration across a semi-permeable membrane.
questions.funFact: Salmon and eels switch between fresh and salt water by remodelling their gills to pump salt in the opposite direction.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: Imagine an ancestral giraffe that spent its whole life stretching its neck to reach high leaves.
questions.question: Would all that stretching give its calves longer necks?
questions.reveal: No; stretching doesn't change the genes passed on.
questions.explanation: The idea that traits acquired during life get inherited was popular before Darwin. But stretching changes your body, not the DNA in your eggs or sperm. Evolution works differently: giraffes naturally varied in neck length, and individuals with slightly longer necks may have survived or reproduced a little better, passing on their genes. Over many generations, the average shifted.
questions.intuitionTrap: It feels intuitive that effort and use should shape what we pass on.
questions.principle: Natural selection acts on inherited variation; traits acquired during life are not generally inherited.
questions.funFact: Despite their length, giraffe necks have seven vertebrae, the same number as yours.
questions.caveat: Biologists still debate why giraffe necks got so long: competing for high leaves and males fighting with their necks are both proposed.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: You breathe fast and deep for a couple of minutes while sitting still.
questions.question: What happens to the carbon dioxide level in your blood?
questions.explanation: Fast breathing flushes CO₂ out of your lungs faster than your cells produce it, so blood CO₂ drops. Oxygen barely changes, because your blood is normally already 95–99% saturated with it. Low CO₂ makes blood more alkaline and narrows blood vessels in the brain, which is why over-breathing causes dizziness and tingling fingers. Your urge to breathe is driven mainly by rising CO₂, not falling oxygen.
questions.intuitionTrap: Breathing harder feels like it should mainly pump in more oxygen.
questions.principle: Ventilation sets blood CO₂; blood oxygen is already near saturation at rest.
questions.funFact: Breathing into a paper bag was the old remedy for over-breathing, but doctors now generally advise against it.
questions.caveat: Hyperventilating before swimming underwater is dangerous: it suppresses the urge to breathe and can cause blackout without warning.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: A mouse's heart beats about 600 times a minute and it lives about two to three years. An elephant's beats about 30 times a minute and it lives about 60 years.
questions.question: Over a whole lifetime, how do their total heartbeats compare?
questions.reveal: Roughly similar: around a billion each.
questions.explanation: Do the arithmetic: 600 beats a minute for 2.5 years is about 0.8 billion beats; 30 a minute for 60 years is about 0.95 billion. Across many mammals, heart rate slows and lifespan lengthens with body size in roughly matching proportions, so lifetime heartbeats land in the same ballpark. Small animals live fast and die young; big ones run slower and longer.
questions.intuitionTrap: A racing mouse heart feels like it must rack up vastly more beats.
questions.principle: Many physiological rates scale with body size in predictable ways (allometric scaling).
questions.funFact: A hummingbird's heart can beat over 1,000 times a minute when it's active.
questions.caveat: It's a rough pattern with exceptions: humans manage around 2.5–3 billion beats, well above the mammal trend.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: A regular gym-goer stops exercising for several weeks.
questions.question: What happens to their muscle cells?
questions.reveal: They shrink, but stay muscle cells.
questions.explanation: Muscle and fat are completely different tissues, and one can't turn into the other. Without training, muscle fibres shrink (atrophy) as the body breaks down some of their proteins. If the person keeps eating the same amount while burning less, their fat cells may grow at the same time, which creates the illusion that 'muscle turned to fat'.
questions.intuitionTrap: Watching a body change shape suggests one tissue is transforming into the other.
questions.principle: Muscle fibres atrophy with disuse; fat cells store excess energy. They are separate cell types.
questions.funFact: Trained muscle fibres seem to keep many of the extra nuclei they gained, which may be one reason regaining strength is often faster than building it the first time.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: You carry a leafy plant from bright sunlight into a completely dark cupboard.
questions.question: When does it stop releasing oxygen?
questions.explanation: The oxygen plants release comes from splitting water molecules, and that step is powered directly by light. Turn off the light and water-splitting stops almost at once. The sugar-building part of photosynthesis coasts briefly on leftover chemical energy, but it releases no oxygen. Meanwhile the plant keeps respiring, burning sugar and consuming oxygen, day and night. In darkness, a plant is a net oxygen consumer.
questions.intuitionTrap: We picture plants as oxygen machines that run around the clock.
questions.principle: Photosynthetic oxygen is produced only by the light-dependent reactions; respiration continues regardless of light.
questions.funFact: Roughly half of the oxygen produced on Earth comes from microscopic ocean plankton rather than land plants.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: You compare the DNA in a skin cell and a brain neuron from the same person.
questions.question: How do their genomes compare?
questions.explanation: Nearly every cell in your body carries the same genome. What makes a neuron a neuron is which genes are switched on: it reads the genes for neurotransmitter machinery, while a skin cell reads genes for keratin and switches the neuron genes off. Gene regulation, not different DNA, is what builds different cell types.
questions.intuitionTrap: Cells that look and behave so differently seem like they must run on different instructions.
questions.principle: Cell types differ in gene expression, not (mostly) in the DNA they contain.
questions.funFact: Dolly the sheep was cloned in 1996 from an adult udder cell, proving a specialised cell still holds a complete set of instructions.
questions.caveat: Mature red blood cells lose their nucleus, some immune cells rearrange parts of their DNA, and every cell picks up a few random mutations.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: A sea star loses one of its arms to a predator. The arm drifts away on its own.
questions.question: Could that detached arm grow into a whole new sea star?
options: Yes, any piece of any sea star
questions.explanation: Almost all sea stars can regrow a lost arm, which takes months to a year. Whether a lost arm can rebuild a whole animal depends on the species. Many need part of the central disc attached, but some, such as Linckia, can regenerate a complete sea star from a single arm, passing through a 'comet' stage of one big arm with tiny new ones sprouting from it.
questions.intuitionTrap: Regeneration feels like an all-or-nothing superpower, either total or impossible.
questions.principle: Regenerative ability varies between species and depends on which tissues remain.
questions.funFact: Some sea stars reproduce on purpose by splitting their own bodies in two.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: An acorn grows into a huge oak tree weighing several tonnes.
questions.question: Where did most of the tree's dry mass come from?
questions.explanation: Wood is mostly cellulose, built from carbon, oxygen and hydrogen. The carbon and most of the oxygen come from CO₂ the leaves pull out of the air during photosynthesis. Water supplies the hydrogen, and the soil provides only a few per cent as minerals such as nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. A tree is largely solidified air.
questions.intuitionTrap: Plants grow out of the ground, so the ground seems like the obvious source.
questions.principle: Photosynthesis fixes atmospheric carbon dioxide into sugars that build plant biomass.
questions.funFact: In the 1600s, Jan Baptist van Helmont grew a willow for five years in a pot of soil that lost only about 60 grams.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: The veins on your wrist look blue through your skin.
questions.question: What colour is the blood inside them?
questions.explanation: Blood is always red: bright red when full of oxygen, darker red after delivering some of it. Veins look blue because of how light travels through skin. Red light penetrates deeper and is strongly absorbed by blood in the vein, so less red comes back from that spot, while bluish light scattered by the overlying tissue still returns. Your brain reads the vein as blue by comparison with the skin around it.
questions.intuitionTrap: Textbook diagrams colour veins blue, and so does our own skin.
questions.principle: The colour we see depends on which wavelengths are absorbed and scattered back, not just on the object's own colour.
questions.funFact: Some animals really do have blue blood: octopuses and horseshoe crabs use copper-based haemocyanin instead of iron-based haemoglobin.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: You pour vinegar onto baking soda in a cup. It fizzes wildly.
questions.question: Does the cup get warmer or colder?
questions.explanation: All that bubbling looks energetic, but this reaction absorbs heat from its surroundings: it's endothermic, so the mixture cools by a few degrees. What drives it forward isn't released heat but disorder. A solid and a liquid produce carbon dioxide gas that escapes, a big increase in entropy, and that is enough to make the reaction run even though it costs heat.
questions.intuitionTrap: Vigorous fizzing feels like an energetic, heat-releasing reaction.
questions.principle: Reactions can be driven by an increase in entropy even when they absorb heat.
questions.funFact: Instant cold packs work on a similar idea: dissolving ammonium nitrate in water absorbs heat and can chill the pack close to freezing.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: People often say that energy is 'stored in chemical bonds' and released when fuel burns or ATP is used.
questions.question: When a chemical bond breaks, what happens to energy?
questions.reveal: Breaking a bond always absorbs energy.
questions.explanation: Pulling bonded atoms apart always takes energy. Energy is released when new bonds form. Burning fuel releases energy because the bonds in the products, carbon dioxide and water, are stronger than the bonds broken in the fuel and oxygen, so forming them gives back more energy than breaking the old ones cost. The energy is in the overall rearrangement, not in any single bond snapping.
questions.intuitionTrap: The phrase 'energy stored in bonds' suggests that breaking them sets the energy free.
questions.principle: Bond breaking is endothermic and bond forming is exothermic; a reaction's energy change is the difference.
questions.funFact: It's the same with magnets: separating two stuck magnets takes effort, and the energy comes out when they snap together.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: A reversible reaction has reached equilibrium. You add a catalyst that speeds up the reaction.
questions.question: What happens to the amount of product?
questions.explanation: A catalyst lowers the energy barrier for the reaction, and the barrier is the same hill whichever way you cross it. So it speeds up the forward and reverse reactions by exactly the same factor. It gets a reaction to equilibrium faster, but it cannot move where that equilibrium sits. If it could, you could build a perpetual-motion machine by adding and removing catalyst.
questions.intuitionTrap: If something speeds up a reaction, it feels like it should produce more of the product.
questions.principle: Catalysts change the rate of reaching equilibrium, never the equilibrium position.
questions.funFact: The catalysts in the Haber process that makes ammonia for fertiliser help feed billions of people, but they only speed it up; temperature and pressure decide the yield.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: A cook chills an onion in the fridge for half an hour before chopping it, and cries much less.
questions.question: Why does the cold help?
options: Cold slows the reaction and evaporation
questions.reveal: Cold slows both the reaction and the evaporation.
questions.explanation: An intact onion contains no tear gas. Cutting breaks open cells and lets enzymes react with sulfur compounds, producing a volatile irritant that drifts up and stimulates nerves in your eyes. Like most reactions, these enzyme steps slow down in the cold, and the irritant evaporates more slowly too. Less of it reaches your eyes, so fewer tears.
questions.intuitionTrap: It seems like the chemical must be sitting in the onion already, waiting to escape.
questions.principle: Reaction and evaporation rates both drop as temperature falls.
questions.funFact: Researchers have bred 'tearless' onions with much lower levels of the compounds that start the reaction.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: You take a strong acid at pH 2 and dilute it with water to ten times its original volume.
questions.question: What is its new pH?
questions.explanation: The pH scale is logarithmic: each step of 1 means a tenfold change in hydrogen-ion concentration. Diluting tenfold cuts the hydrogen ions to a tenth, so the pH rises by exactly one, from 2 to 3. The acid is still acidic; it would take another hundredfold dilution to reach pH 5.
questions.intuitionTrap: We expect a 'ten times' change to move a number by ten, or forget that pH goes up as acidity goes down.
questions.principle: pH = −log₁₀[H⁺], so a tenfold dilution of a strong acid raises the pH by 1.
questions.funFact: Lemon juice (about pH 2) has around ten thousand times more hydrogen ions than black coffee (about pH 5–6).
questions.caveat: No amount of dilution makes an acid basic: as it approaches neutral, water's own ions take over and the pH levels off near 7.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: A reaction A + B ⇌ C has settled into equilibrium in a sealed flask of solution. You inject extra A.
questions.question: Which way does the equilibrium shift?
options: Toward making more A and B
questions.explanation: Equilibrium isn't a frozen state: forward and reverse reactions keep running at equal rates. Adding A speeds up the forward reaction, because more A molecules are now colliding with B, so for a while C is made faster than it breaks down. The system shifts toward C until the two rates balance again, using up some of the A you added.
questions.intuitionTrap: 'Equilibrium' sounds static, as if nothing is happening any more.
questions.principle: Le Chatelier's principle: a system at equilibrium partly counteracts a change imposed on it.
questions.funFact: Your blood uses this constantly: when you exercise and make extra CO₂, its carbonic-acid equilibrium shifts to buffer the change in acidity.
questions.caveat: Adding more of a pure solid, such as extra limestone in CaCO₃ ⇌ CaO + CO₂, doesn't shift the equilibrium at all.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: You push a zinc-coated nail and a copper coin into a lemon, wire them up, and a tiny LED glows.
questions.question: Where does the electrical energy mainly come from?
questions.reveal: From the zinc being slowly eaten away.
questions.explanation: The lemon is mostly a convenient electrolyte, a salty, acidic liquid that lets ions move. The energy comes from the zinc: it gives up electrons and slowly dissolves (it is oxidised). Those electrons flow through the wire to the copper, where hydrogen ions from the juice pick them up. The copper isn't used up at all. Swap the lemon for a potato or salty water and it still works.
questions.intuitionTrap: The lemon is the star of the demo, so it gets the credit.
questions.principle: Batteries convert the chemical energy of a redox reaction into electrical energy.
questions.funFact: It takes several lemons wired in series to light even one small LED.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: Gold is famous for being unreactive: it doesn't tarnish even after thousands of years. Now you divide gold into particles just a few nanometres across.
questions.question: Can those tiny gold particles act as a powerful chemical catalyst?
options: Yes, they can be very active
Only if the gold is molten
questions.reveal: Yes: nanoscale gold can be a highly active catalyst.
questions.explanation: In a particle only a few nanometres wide, a large share of atoms sit on surfaces, edges and corners, where their electrons behave differently from atoms buried inside bulk metal. In the 1980s, chemist Masatake Haruta showed that gold nanoparticles on a metal-oxide support can catalyse reactions such as turning carbon monoxide into carbon dioxide, even below room temperature. Bulk gold does nothing of the kind.
questions.intuitionTrap: We treat 'unreactive' as a fixed property of an element, whatever its size.
questions.principle: At the nanoscale, surface atoms dominate and properties can differ sharply from the bulk material.
questions.funFact: Gold nanoparticles aren't even gold-coloured: they look red or purple, and colour some medieval stained glass.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: The oceans have absorbed a large share of the CO₂ released by burning fossil fuels, a process called ocean acidification.
questions.question: Has seawater actually become acidic (pH below 7)?
questions.reveal: No; it's still basic, just less so.
questions.explanation: Surface seawater has a pH of about 8.1, which is basic. Dissolved CO₂ forms carbonic acid, which nudges the pH downward: it has fallen by about 0.1 since pre-industrial times. Because the scale is logarithmic, that small number means about 25–30% more hydrogen ions. 'Acidification' describes the direction of change, not the destination, and even this shift makes it harder for corals and shellfish to build their shells.
questions.intuitionTrap: The word 'acidification' suggests the water has already become an acid.
questions.principle: pH is logarithmic, and 'acidifying' means moving toward lower pH, not crossing below 7.
questions.funFact: Some shellfish farms on the US Pacific coast have adjusted how they raise oyster larvae because of more corrosive seawater.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: You open a bottle of perfume in one corner of a closed room where the air feels still. A few minutes later, someone on the far side smells it.
questions.question: What mostly carried the smell across the room?
questions.explanation: Diffusion is real but painfully slow over long distances. Each molecule zig-zags randomly, colliding with air molecules billions of times a second, so the distance it spreads grows only with the square root of time. Crossing five metres by diffusion alone would take weeks. Even a 'still' room has slow drafts from warm bodies, lamps and windows, and those currents sweep the scent across in minutes.
questions.intuitionTrap: Textbooks use perfume as the classic diffusion example, so we credit diffusion for the whole trip.
questions.principle: Diffusion distance grows with the square root of time; over room-sized distances, convection dominates.
questions.funFact: Gas molecules at room temperature move at hundreds of metres per second; they just never get far before changing direction.

goDeeper.text: With a diffusion coefficient of about 0.07 cm²/s and L = 500 cm, t ≈ 1.8 million seconds: about three weeks.

questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: You grind a sugar cube into a very fine powder.
questions.question: Has it become a more reactive substance?
options: It reacts faster; its chemistry is unchanged
questions.reveal: It reacts faster, but its chemistry is unchanged.
questions.explanation: Grinding creates vastly more surface area, so anything that happens at the surface, such as dissolving or burning, goes much faster. Clouds of fine flour or sugar dust can even explode. But the molecules are identical: the same reactions are possible, they release the same energy per gram, and they reach the same equilibrium. Faster is not the same as more reactive.
questions.intuitionTrap: Seeing powder react violently suggests the substance itself has changed.
questions.principle: Surface area changes the rate of a reaction, not its thermodynamics.
questions.funFact: Dust explosions are a real hazard in flour mills, grain silos and sugar refineries.
questions.caveat: At the nanoscale, particles a few billionths of a metre across, surface atoms dominate and some materials do behave differently.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: An iron nail is left outside until it has completely rusted. You carefully collect every flake of rust.
questions.question: How does the weight of the rust compare with the original nail?
questions.explanation: Rusting isn't iron crumbling away; it's iron combining with oxygen and water from the air. Those extra atoms add mass, so the rust (a hydrated iron oxide) weighs noticeably more than the iron did, roughly 40% more for plain iron oxide and more still with the water. Mass is still conserved overall: the extra came out of the air.
questions.intuitionTrap: Rust looks like decay, and decay feels like losing material.
questions.principle: In a chemical reaction mass is conserved; oxidation adds oxygen atoms to the metal.
questions.funFact: Antoine Lavoisier used careful weighing of metals heated in air to help overturn the 'phlogiston' theory of burning in the 1770s.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: You stir a big spoonful of salt into a glass of water.
questions.question: What happens to the temperature at which the water freezes?
questions.explanation: To freeze, water molecules must lock into the orderly lattice of an ice crystal. Dissolved salt ions get in the way: they dilute the water and make it harder for molecules to join the crystal, so the mixture must get colder before it freezes. The effect depends on how many dissolved particles there are, not what they are, which is why sugar works too, just less strongly per spoonful.
questions.intuitionTrap: Adding 'stuff' to water feels like it should make it thicker and quicker to freeze.
questions.principle: Dissolved particles lower a solvent's freezing point (freezing-point depression).
questions.funFact: Seawater freezes at about −1.9 °C, and road salt stops being much use below roughly −10 °C.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: You sprinkle a handful of salt over a bowl of crushed ice and stir.
questions.question: What happens to the temperature of the icy mix?
questions.explanation: Salt lowers the freezing point, so the ice starts melting even though it's below 0 °C. Melting needs energy, and the quickest place to get it is from the mixture itself, so the temperature drops. A salt-and-ice mix can reach about −20 °C, which is how old-fashioned ice-cream makers freeze cream without a freezer.
questions.intuitionTrap: Salt 'melts ice' on roads, so it feels like it must be warming things up.
questions.principle: Melting absorbs latent heat; salt lets ice melt at lower temperatures and so pulls heat from the mix.
questions.funFact: The lowest temperature a salt-and-water mix can reach while staying liquid is about −21 °C.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: Greasy hands won't come clean under running water, but a little soap gets the grease off easily.
questions.question: What does the soap actually do?
options: Grabs grease and water at once
questions.reveal: Its molecules grab grease with one end and water with the other.
questions.explanation: Water and oil don't mix, so water alone just slides over grease. A soap molecule has a long oil-loving tail and a water-loving head. The tails bury themselves in the grease while the heads stay in the water, and the grease breaks up into tiny droplets wrapped in soap, called micelles, which rinse away. The grease isn't destroyed, just escorted off.
questions.intuitionTrap: 'Cleaning' sounds like the dirt is being chemically broken down.
questions.principle: Surfactants have a water-loving head and an oil-loving tail, letting oil be carried away in water.
questions.funFact: Soap also destroys many viruses, including flu and coronaviruses, by tearing apart their fatty outer envelope.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: You put a sealed can of fizzy drink in the freezer to chill it quickly, then forget about it overnight.
questions.question: What's most likely to have happened by morning?
questions.explanation: At first, cooling actually lowers the pressure a little: cold liquid holds more dissolved CO₂ and cold gas pushes less. The trouble starts when it freezes. Water expands by about 9% as it turns to ice, and ice can't hold dissolved gas, so CO₂ is squeezed out of the freezing liquid into an ever-smaller space. The pressure climbs until the can bulges, the lid pops or a seam splits.
questions.intuitionTrap: Cold usually makes things contract, so freezing seems like it should shrink everything.
questions.principle: Water expands on freezing, and gases are expelled from growing ice crystals.
questions.funFact: The same expansion splits rocks: water seeping into cracks freezes, wedges them open and slowly breaks mountains apart.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: A fluffy white cumulus cloud, about a kilometre across, drifts overhead.
questions.question: Roughly how much does the water in it weigh?
questions.explanation: A cumulus cloud holds about half a gram of liquid water per cubic metre. A cloud a kilometre across contains about a billion cubic metres, so that's roughly 500 tonnes of water. It doesn't fall because the droplets are tiny, about a hundredth of a millimetre across. Air drag lets them sink only about a centimetre per second, and rising air currents easily hold them up.
questions.intuitionTrap: Clouds look weightless, so they seem to contain almost nothing.
questions.principle: Tiny droplets have very low terminal velocities, so large masses of water can stay suspended.
questions.funFact: A big thunderstorm cloud can hold hundreds of thousands of tonnes of water.

goDeeper.text: That's 500 tonnes. For tiny droplets, terminal velocity grows with the square of the radius (Stokes' law), so cloud droplets sink at only about a centimetre per second.

questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: In many deserts, scorching afternoons are followed by surprisingly cold nights.
questions.question: What's the main reason the temperature drops so far?
options: The sand reflects heat at night
Dry, clear air lets heat escape
Cold winds blow in from mountains
questions.reveal: Dry, clear air lets heat radiate straight out to space.
questions.explanation: At night the ground cools by radiating infrared heat upward. Water vapour and clouds absorb much of that infrared and send some back down, acting like a blanket. Desert air is dry and the skies are usually clear, so the heat escapes straight to space. Dry sand also stores relatively little heat, so the surface cools quickly once the Sun goes down.
questions.intuitionTrap: Hot places seem like they should stay hot.
questions.principle: Water vapour is a strong absorber of infrared radiation; dry, clear air lets surfaces cool rapidly.
questions.funFact: On clear nights, even in non-desert climates, frost can form on cars while the air temperature is still above freezing.
questions.source: Standard earth science references (e.g. NOAA, USGS, OpenStax)
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: Earth's natural greenhouse effect keeps the planet about 33 °C warmer than it would otherwise be.
questions.question: Which gas contributes the most to that natural greenhouse effect?
questions.explanation: Water vapour accounts for about half of today's greenhouse effect, clouds about a quarter, and CO₂ about a fifth. But water vapour acts as a feedback, not a control knob: how much the air can hold depends on temperature, and excess vapour rains out within days. CO₂ stays in the air for centuries. When CO₂ warms the planet, the air holds more water vapour, which amplifies that warming.
questions.intuitionTrap: Carbon dioxide dominates climate news, so it seems like it must be the biggest absorber.
questions.principle: Long-lived gases like CO₂ set the temperature; short-lived water vapour responds to it and amplifies the change.
questions.funFact: Without any greenhouse effect, Earth's average surface temperature would be around −18 °C instead of about 15 °C.
questions.source: Schmidt et al. (2010), Journal of Geophysical Research
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: Compare the air inside a lightning bolt with the visible surface of the Sun.
questions.question: Which is hotter?
questions.reveal: The lightning bolt, by about five times.
questions.explanation: A lightning channel briefly heats the air to around 30,000 °C, roughly five times hotter than the Sun's visible surface at about 5,500 °C. It's only a few centimetres wide and lasts a tiny fraction of a second, which is why it doesn't melt everything around it. That sudden heating makes the air expand explosively, and the shock wave is what you hear as thunder.
questions.intuitionTrap: Nothing on Earth feels like it could rival the Sun.
questions.principle: Temperature is about energy concentration: a small, brief event can be far hotter than a vast, steady one.
questions.funFact: Lightning strikes Earth roughly 40–50 times every second, worldwide.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: Imagine Earth's atmosphere were suddenly stripped away, leaving the oceans exposed to near-vacuum.
questions.question: What happens to the boiling point of the water?
questions.explanation: Water boils when its vapour pressure matches the pressure pushing down on it. Remove the air and that pressure drops toward zero, so the boiling point plunges and oceans at everyday temperatures would start to boil. Boiling carries heat away, so the water left behind would chill and even freeze while still bubbling. Eventually the vapour itself would build up into a thin new atmosphere and the boiling would stop.
questions.intuitionTrap: Boiling is associated with heat, not with pressure.
questions.principle: A liquid's boiling point depends on the pressure above it.
questions.funFact: On the summit of Everest, water boils at only about 70 °C.
questions.source: Standard earth science references (e.g. NOAA, USGS, OpenStax)
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: The continents sit on tectonic plates that slowly move across Earth's surface.
questions.question: About how fast do they move?
questions.reveal: About as fast as your fingernails grow.
questions.explanation: Most plates move a few centimetres per year, from about 2 to 10 cm, similar to the rate fingernails grow. GPS stations measure this directly today. It sounds trivial, but over 100 million years, 5 cm per year adds up to 5,000 km, enough to open an entire ocean. The Atlantic has been widening like this since the supercontinent Pangaea broke apart.
questions.intuitionTrap: Continents feel permanently fixed, so any motion seems either impossible or catastrophic.
questions.principle: Slow, steady rates add up to enormous distances over geological time.
questions.funFact: India is still pushing north into Asia at a few centimetres a year, which keeps raising the Himalayas.
questions.source: Standard earth science references (e.g. NOAA, USGS, OpenStax)
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: One earthquake measures magnitude 6. Another measures magnitude 7.
questions.question: How much more energy does the magnitude 7 quake release?
questions.explanation: Earthquake magnitude is a logarithmic scale. Each whole step means about 10 times larger ground motion on a seismograph and about 32 times more energy released. So a magnitude 8 releases about 1,000 times the energy of a magnitude 6. A difference of 'just one point' is enormous.
questions.intuitionTrap: Numbers that differ by one feel like they should describe similar events.
questions.principle: On the magnitude scale, energy grows by a factor of about 10^1.5 ≈ 32 per unit step.
questions.funFact: The 1960 Chile earthquake, magnitude 9.5, is the largest ever recorded.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: Picture a medium-sized raindrop partway through its fall from a cloud.
questions.question: What shape is it?
questions.reveal: Round, with a flattened bottom like a burger bun.
questions.explanation: Surface tension pulls small drops into near-perfect spheres. As drops get bigger and fall faster, air pressure pushes up on their undersides and flattens them, giving a shape more like a hamburger bun than a teardrop. Very large drops flatten so much that they break apart into smaller ones. The pointed teardrop is an artist's invention, perhaps borrowed from drips leaving a tap.
questions.intuitionTrap: Every cartoon and weather icon draws raindrops as teardrops.
questions.principle: Surface tension and air pressure together set the shape of a falling drop.
questions.funFact: Raindrops rarely grow beyond about 5 mm across before air resistance breaks them up.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: Rivers taste fresh, yet the oceans they flow into are salty.
questions.question: Where does the ocean's salt mostly come from?
questions.explanation: Rain is slightly acidic and slowly dissolves minerals from rocks. Rivers carry tiny amounts of these dissolved salts, too little to taste, into the sea. Evaporation lifts pure water out of the ocean but leaves the salts behind, and over hundreds of millions of years they've accumulated. Hydrothermal vents on the seafloor add some dissolved minerals too.
questions.intuitionTrap: If rivers taste fresh, they seem unable to be the source of all that salt.
questions.principle: Evaporation removes water but not dissolved salts, so salts accumulate where water only leaves by evaporating.
questions.funFact: The same process makes landlocked lakes like the Dead Sea far saltier than the ocean.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: Suppose all the floating Arctic sea ice melted completely.
questions.question: How much would that alone raise global sea level?
questions.explanation: Sea ice is already floating, so it already displaces its own weight of seawater, just like an ice cube in a drink. When it melts, it fills almost exactly the space it was displacing. Ice on land is different: melting glaciers and the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets adds new water to the ocean and does raise sea levels, as does seawater expanding as it warms.
questions.intuitionTrap: 'Melting ice' and 'rising seas' are so often linked that all ice seems to count.
questions.principle: Melting floating ice barely changes water level; melting land ice adds water to the ocean.
questions.funFact: If Greenland's ice sheet melted entirely, global sea level would rise by about 7 metres.
questions.caveat: Strictly, freshwater ice melting into salty seawater raises the level a tiny amount, because meltwater is slightly less dense than seawater.
questions.source: Standard earth science references (e.g. NOAA, USGS, OpenStax)
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: A popular claim says water drains clockwise in one hemisphere and anticlockwise in the other.
questions.question: Does Earth's rotation decide which way your sink swirls?
options: No, the effect is far too weak
questions.reveal: No; at sink size the effect is far too weak.
questions.explanation: The Coriolis effect is real and steers hurricanes, which spin anticlockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern. But its strength depends on scale and time. Over a hurricane hundreds of kilometres wide lasting days, it dominates. In a sink, the shape of the basin and leftover swirls from filling it are thousands of times stronger, so drains can go either way in either hemisphere.
questions.intuitionTrap: If it works for hurricanes, it seems like it should work for any swirling water.
questions.principle: The Coriolis effect matters only for motions that are large or slow enough for Earth's rotation to act on them.
questions.funFact: Careful experiments using large, still tanks of water left to settle for a day have detected the true Coriolis direction.
questions.source: Standard earth science references (e.g. NOAA, USGS, OpenStax)
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: Air scatters short wavelengths of light most strongly, and violet light has an even shorter wavelength than blue.
questions.question: So why does the sky look blue rather than violet?
options: Less violet light, weaker violet vision
questions.reveal: Sunlight has less violet, and our eyes are less sensitive to it.
questions.explanation: Air molecules scatter shorter wavelengths more strongly, so violet really is scattered even more than blue. But sunlight contains less violet than blue to begin with, and our eyes respond only weakly to violet. The colour-sensing cones in our eyes combine the scattered mix of violet, blue and some green into the sensation we call sky blue.
questions.intuitionTrap: If scattering favours short wavelengths, the shortest visible one should win.
questions.principle: Perceived colour depends on the light spectrum and on the sensitivity of our eyes, not just on the physics of scattering.
questions.funFact: Scattered skylight is also partly polarised, and bees use that polarisation pattern to navigate.
questions.source: Standard earth science references (e.g. NOAA, USGS, OpenStax)
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: You see a flash of lightning and count 9 seconds before you hear the thunder.
questions.question: Roughly how far away was the strike?
questions.explanation: The light reaches you almost instantly, but sound plods along at about 343 metres per second. In 9 seconds sound travels roughly 3 kilometres, so that's how far away the strike was. The handy rule: divide the seconds by 3 to get kilometres. If the gap is under about 30 seconds, the storm is close enough that you should already be indoors.
questions.intuitionTrap: It's easy to treat the flash and the bang as one event happening together.
questions.principle: Light travels about a million times faster than sound in air, so the delay measures distance.
questions.funFact: Thunder is rarely heard beyond about 15–25 km, even though lightning can be seen much farther away.
questions.source: Standard earth science references (e.g. NOAA, USGS, OpenStax)
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: A tsunami is crossing the deep open ocean. A ship far from shore is directly in its path.
questions.question: What does the ship experience as the wave passes?
questions.reveal: A gentle rise and fall it might not even notice.
questions.explanation: In deep water a tsunami may be less than a metre high, but its wavelength can be hundreds of kilometres, so a ship rises and falls gently over many minutes. The wave travels astonishingly fast, around 700 km/h in 4 km of water. Only when it reaches shallow coastal water does it slow down, bunch up and grow many metres tall.
questions.intuitionTrap: We picture the wall of water seen at the coast as existing all the way across the ocean.
questions.principle: Shallow-water waves slow and grow taller as depth decreases (wave shoaling).
questions.funFact: That's why ships in harbour are often ordered out to deep water when a tsunami warning is issued.

questions.scenario: A moving bicycle stays upright far more easily than one that is standing still.
questions.question: What is mainly responsible?
options: It steers itself under its lean
questions.reveal: It steers itself back under its lean.
questions.explanation: Gyroscopic effects exist but are small. A moving bike stays up mainly because, when it starts to lean, its front wheel turns toward the lean, steering the wheels back under the centre of mass, much as you balance a broom on your palm by moving your hand. In 2011, researchers built a bicycle with extra counter-spinning wheels to cancel the gyroscopic effect, and it still balanced itself.
questions.intuitionTrap: Spinning wheels look like gyroscopes, so gyroscopes get the credit.
questions.principle: Bicycle stability comes mostly from steering geometry and mass distribution that steer the bike into its fall.
questions.funFact: Riders do the same thing unconsciously: to turn left, you briefly steer right so the bike leans left.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: On a hot, sunny, breezy day in the desert, you wear a loose black robe instead of a loose white one.
questions.question: Will you necessarily end up hotter?
options: No, black always keeps you cooler
questions.explanation: A black robe does absorb more sunlight, and its outer surface gets noticeably hotter. But a 1980 study of Bedouin robes found that the heat reaching the wearer's body was about the same with black and white. The hotter fabric warms the air beneath it, which rises and pulls in fresh air through the loose weave and openings, carrying extra heat away, especially when there's a breeze.
questions.intuitionTrap: 'Black absorbs heat' is true, so it seems to settle the question.
questions.principle: What reaches your skin depends on absorption, airflow and convection together, not colour alone.
questions.funFact: The researchers even tested robes on volunteers standing in the Negev desert at midday.
questions.caveat: Tight black clothing in still air is a different story: then it can make you noticeably warmer.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: A driver who brakes hard from 50 km/h stops in a certain distance after the brakes bite.
questions.question: From 100 km/h, on the same road with the same brakes, how far does the braking take?
questions.explanation: Brakes remove kinetic energy, and kinetic energy grows with the square of speed. Double the speed and there's four times as much energy to get rid of, so with the same braking force the car needs about four times the distance. On top of that, the distance covered during the driver's reaction time simply doubles. Speed matters far more than it feels like it should.
questions.intuitionTrap: We expect stopping distance to grow in step with speed: twice as fast, twice as far.
questions.principle: Kinetic energy = ½mv², so braking distance grows with the square of speed.
questions.funFact: Hitting something at 60 km/h carries about the same energy as falling from a 14-metre building, roughly four storeys.

questions.scenario: Chain round. You drop a single ice cube into a glass of room-temperature water.
questions.question: What does the cube do first?
questions.reveal: It floats, with about nine-tenths underwater.
questions.explanation: Water is unusual: its solid is less dense than its liquid. As water freezes, its molecules lock into an open hexagonal lattice held apart by hydrogen bonds, so ice is about 9% less dense than liquid water. That's enough to float, but only just, so roughly nine-tenths of the cube sits below the waterline, exactly as with an iceberg.
questions.intuitionTrap: Solids are usually denser than their liquids, so a frozen lump seems like it should sink.
questions.principle: Ice is less dense than liquid water, and a floating object sinks until it displaces its own weight.
questions.funFact: If ice sank, lakes would freeze from the bottom up and much of the life in them could not survive winter.
questions.source: Standard physics and chemistry of everyday life
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: Chain round, finale. You marked the water level on the glass just after the ice cube went in. Now the cube has completely melted.
questions.question: Compared with your mark, where is the water level now?
questions.explanation: While floating, the cube displaced exactly its own weight of water. Melting turns it into exactly that weight of water, which fills the space it was displacing. The part above the waterline only existed because ice is less dense; once it's liquid, that extra volume disappears. So the level ends where it started after the cube went in.
questions.intuitionTrap: The visible ice above the waterline looks like extra water still to come.
questions.principle: A floating object displaces its own weight of liquid (Archimedes' principle).
questions.funFact: You've now followed the cube from floating, through sinking meltwater, to a level that never moved.
questions.source: Standard physics and chemistry of everyday life
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: Chain round, continued. As the floating cube melts, it releases a trickle of very cold meltwater, close to 0 °C.
questions.question: Where does that cold meltwater go?
questions.explanation: Cold liquid water near 0 °C is denser than room-temperature water, so the meltwater sinks, pulling warmer water in to replace it. That sets up a slow circulation that carries heat to the cube and speeds its melting. You can see it by using a coloured ice cube: streamers of colour drift downward. Ice floats, but its meltwater dives.
questions.intuitionTrap: Since the ice floats, it seems like its meltwater should float too.
questions.principle: Between about 4 °C and room temperature, colder water is denser than warmer water.
questions.funFact: This density quirk keeps the bottom of deep lakes at about 4 °C all winter.
questions.caveat: Water is densest at about 4 °C; in water colder than that, meltwater would rise instead.
questions.source: Standard physics and chemistry of everyday life
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: You pour an ice-cold drink into a glass. A few minutes later, the outside of the glass is wet.
questions.question: Where did that water come from?
questions.reveal: From water vapour in the surrounding air.
questions.explanation: Air always contains invisible water vapour. When air touches the cold surface of the glass, it cools below its 'dew point', the temperature at which it can't hold all its vapour, and the excess condenses into droplets. Glass is waterproof, so nothing leaks through. On a humid day the glass gets wetter; in a dry room it may stay almost dry.
questions.intuitionTrap: Water on the outside of a container full of liquid looks like a leak.
questions.principle: Air cooled below its dew point releases water vapour as liquid condensation.
questions.funFact: It's the same physics that makes morning dew, fog and the drips from an air conditioner.
questions.source: Standard physics and chemistry of everyday life
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: Aluminium foil has a shiny side and a dull side.
questions.question: For ordinary cooking, does it matter which side faces the food?
questions.explanation: The two sides differ only because of how foil is made. In the final rolling step, two sheets pass through the rollers together: the sides touching the polished rollers come out shiny, and the sides touching each other come out matte. The difference in how much heat they reflect is small, so for normal cooking it makes no meaningful difference which way you wrap.
questions.intuitionTrap: Two visibly different sides seem like they must have two different jobs.
questions.principle: Surface finish from manufacturing slightly changes reflectivity, but the effect on cooking is negligible.
questions.funFact: Household foil is typically less than a fiftieth of a millimetre thick.
questions.caveat: Non-stick foil is different: it has a coating on one side, which should face the food.
questions.source: Standard physics and chemistry of everyday life
