questions.scenario: On a hot day, you shut yourself in a small, closed room with a refrigerator and leave the fridge door wide open.
questions.question: Over an hour, what happens to the room's temperature?
questions.explanation: A refrigerator doesn't destroy heat; it pumps heat from inside the box out through the coils at the back. With the door open, it's moving heat from the room... into the same room. Meanwhile its motor turns electrical energy into extra heat. Net result: the room gets slightly warmer. Air conditioners only cool a room because they dump their heat outdoors.
questions.intuitionTrap: The cold air pouring out of the door feels like cooling.
questions.principle: Refrigerators are heat pumps; they move heat and add the energy they consume as extra heat.
questions.funFact: The coils on the back of a fridge release more heat than the fridge removes from its contents, because they also dump the motor's energy.
questions.source: Standard physics and chemistry of everyday life
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: A thermometer reads 34 °C on two days. One day is dry; the other is very humid.
questions.question: Why does the humid day feel so much worse?
options: Humid air presses on your skin
questions.reveal: Your sweat can't evaporate as easily.
questions.explanation: Your body's main way of cooling in heat is sweating: as sweat evaporates, it carries heat away from your skin. When the air is already loaded with water vapour, evaporation slows down, so sweat drips instead of cooling you. Your body keeps heating up at the same air temperature. That's why weather services report a 'feels like' or heat index temperature.
questions.intuitionTrap: If the thermometer reads the same, the heat seems like it should feel the same.
questions.principle: Evaporation absorbs latent heat; it slows when the surrounding air is close to saturated.
questions.funFact: Dogs pant for the same reason: evaporating water from their tongue and airways cools them down.
questions.source: Standard physics and chemistry of everyday life
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: A glass is filled to the very brim with water, with ice cubes floating in it.
questions.question: When all the ice melts, what happens?
questions.reveal: The level stays the same; nothing overflows.
questions.explanation: Floating ice displaces exactly its own weight of water. When it melts, it becomes exactly that weight of liquid water, which fills precisely the space the ice was pushing aside below the waterline. The bit of ice poking above the surface is just making up for ice being less dense than water. So the level doesn't change.
questions.intuitionTrap: The ice sticking up above the surface looks like extra volume waiting to spill over.
questions.principle: A floating object displaces its own weight of liquid (Archimedes' principle).
questions.funFact: That's why melting floating sea ice barely raises sea level, while melting land ice does.
questions.caveat: This holds for pure water with freely floating ice; small temperature-related volume changes can nudge it very slightly.
questions.source: Standard physics and chemistry of everyday life

questions.scenario: A metal spoon and a wooden spoon have been lying side by side on a table in the same room all day. You pick up one in each hand.
questions.question: Which spoon is actually colder?
questions.explanation: After hours in the same room, both spoons are at room temperature. The metal feels colder because it conducts heat away from your warm fingers much faster. Your skin doesn't sense temperature directly; it senses how quickly heat is flowing in or out. Wood conducts heat poorly, so the patch you touch quickly warms toward skin temperature and feels neutral.
questions.intuitionTrap: We trust our sense of touch as a thermometer.
questions.principle: Touch senses heat flow, which depends on a material's thermal conductivity, not just its temperature.
questions.funFact: The same effect is why a tiled bathroom floor feels freezing while a rug in the same room feels fine.
questions.source: Standard physics and chemistry of everyday life
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: You microwave a cup of cold liquid water and a block of ice of the same mass, side by side, for the same short time.
questions.question: Which absorbs microwave energy faster?
questions.explanation: Microwaves heat food mainly by making water molecules twist back and forth as the field flips billions of times a second. In liquid water, molecules can rotate fairly freely and absorb that energy well. In ice, they're locked into a crystal and can barely rotate, so ice absorbs microwaves poorly. That's why defrost settings pulse on and off: they let small thawed areas spread heat into frozen parts instead of cooking the edges.
questions.intuitionTrap: If microwaves 'heat water', frozen water seems like it should heat just as well.
questions.principle: Microwave heating depends on how easily molecules can rotate in the oscillating field (dielectric loss).
questions.funFact: Most microwave ovens operate at about 2.45 GHz, the same band as many Wi-Fi networks.
questions.source: Standard physics and chemistry of everyday life
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: Some old church windows are thicker at the bottom than at the top.
questions.question: Is that because glass slowly flows downward over centuries?
options: Yes, glass is a very slow liquid
No, it was made that way
Yes, but only in hot climates
questions.reveal: No; it was made uneven to begin with.
questions.explanation: At room temperature glass is an amorphous solid: its atoms are disordered like a liquid's, but locked in place. Calculations suggest any flow at room temperature would take vastly longer than the age of the universe to notice. Old windowpanes were made by methods such as spinning molten glass into a disc, which produced uneven sheets. Installers often put the thick edge at the bottom, but sometimes at the top or side.
questions.intuitionTrap: Uneven old glass looks like evidence of slow dripping.
questions.principle: Glass is an amorphous solid with an astronomically high viscosity at room temperature.
questions.funFact: Ancient Roman glassware and centuries-old telescope lenses show no sign of sagging.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: Dal that takes an hour in an open pot is ready in minutes in a pressure cooker.
questions.question: Why does the pressure cooker cook so much faster?
questions.reveal: The water inside gets hotter than 100 °C.
questions.explanation: In an open pot, water can't get hotter than its boiling point, about 100 °C at sea level; extra heat just makes more steam. Sealing the lid traps the steam and raises the pressure to roughly double normal air pressure, which pushes the boiling point up to around 120 °C. Cooking reactions speed up a lot with every extra degree, so food softens in a fraction of the time.
questions.intuitionTrap: Pressure itself seems to be doing the cooking.
questions.principle: Higher pressure raises water's boiling point, allowing hotter cooking temperatures.
questions.funFact: Pressure cookers matter even more at altitude, where water in an open pot boils well below 100 °C.
questions.source: Standard physics and chemistry of everyday life
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: You add a spoonful of salt to a big pot of water on the stove before cooking pasta.
questions.question: What does the salt do to the water's boiling point?
questions.reveal: It raises it, but only by a tiny fraction of a degree.
questions.explanation: Dissolved particles make water molecules slightly less likely to escape as vapour, so salt raises the boiling point. But a cooking amount of salt in a big pot raises it by only a small fraction of a degree, so it doesn't speed up or slow down boiling in any useful way. The burst of bubbles when salt hits hot water is just dissolved gas escaping onto the crystals. Salt is for flavour.
questions.intuitionTrap: The fizz when salt goes in looks like it's making the water boil.
questions.principle: Solutes raise a solvent's boiling point in proportion to their concentration (boiling-point elevation).
questions.funFact: To raise water's boiling point by even 1 °C, you'd need roughly 50 grams of salt per litre, saltier than seawater.
questions.source: Standard physics and chemistry of everyday life
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: Soap bubbles shimmer with swirling rainbow colours, even though soapy water is colourless.
questions.question: Where do the colours come from?
questions.reveal: Light reflecting off both surfaces of the film and interfering.
questions.explanation: A bubble's wall is a film only a few hundred nanometres thick. Light reflects from both its outer and inner surfaces, and the two reflections overlap. Depending on the film's thickness, some colours line up and reinforce each other while others cancel out. As the film drains and thins, the colours swirl and shift, and just before popping it can turn almost black.
questions.intuitionTrap: Rainbows are linked with prisms and raindrops, so we assume the same splitting of light.
questions.principle: Thin-film interference: light reflected from two nearby surfaces reinforces or cancels by wavelength.
questions.funFact: The same effect colours oil slicks on wet roads and some beetle shells and butterfly wings.
questions.source: Standard physics and chemistry of everyday life
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: A tennis player hits a ball with heavy topspin, so the top of the ball rotates forward as it flies.
questions.question: Compared with a ball hit the same way with no spin, what does it do?
questions.explanation: A spinning ball drags a thin layer of air around with it. With topspin, the airflow leaving the back of the ball gets deflected upward, and by Newton's third law the ball is pushed downward. This Magnus effect makes topspin shots dive into the court, letting players hit hard and still land the ball in. Backspin does the opposite and makes the ball float.
questions.intuitionTrap: Spin feels like a cosmetic extra that shouldn't change where a ball goes.
questions.principle: The Magnus effect: a spinning ball deflects air to one side and feels a force toward the other.
questions.funFact: Golf balls fly far partly thanks to backspin, which creates lift; their dimples help keep that airflow attached.
questions.source: Standard physics and chemistry of everyday life
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: You fill your car tyres to the right pressure on a warm afternoon. The next morning is much colder.
questions.question: What does the tyre gauge read in the cold morning?
questions.explanation: The air in a tyre is a fixed amount of gas in a nearly fixed volume. Its pressure comes from molecules hitting the tyre walls, and colder molecules move more slowly and hit less hard. So when the temperature drops, the pressure drops with it, by roughly 1 psi for every 5–6 °C. Nothing leaked; check tyre pressures when the tyres are cold for an accurate reading.
questions.intuitionTrap: If no air escaped, the pressure seems like it should stay put.
questions.principle: For a fixed amount of gas in a fixed volume, pressure is proportional to absolute temperature.
questions.funFact: Formula 1 teams warm their tyres in electric blankets before a race partly to get pressures right.
questions.source: Standard physics and chemistry of everyday life
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: Fifty people with ordinary incomes are in a café. A billionaire walks in.
questions.question: What happens to the median income of the people in the café?
questions.explanation: The median is the middle value when everyone is lined up by income. Adding one person at the top just shifts the middle position a fraction of a place, so the median stays almost exactly the same. The mean, on the other hand, shoots up: one billion divided among 51 people adds about twenty million to the average. That's why median income usually tells you more about a typical person.
questions.intuitionTrap: 'Average' and 'median' get treated as the same thing.
questions.principle: The median is robust to extreme values; the mean is not.
questions.funFact: Mean household wealth in many countries is far above the median, because a small group holds a large share of wealth.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored; numerical claims verified by direct computation; pending independent review.

questions.scenario: People walk into a room one at a time. Ignore leap years and twins.
questions.question: How many people need to be there for a better-than-even chance that two share a birthday?
questions.explanation: The trick is counting pairs, not people. With 23 people there are 253 different pairs, and each pair is another chance for a match. The chance that all 23 birthdays are different works out to about 49.3%, so the chance of at least one shared birthday is about 50.7%. With 70 people a match is over 99.9% likely.
questions.intuitionTrap: We imagine someone matching our own birthday, which really does need about 253 people.
questions.principle: The number of pairs grows quadratically with group size, so coincidences become likely surprisingly fast.
questions.funFact: In a typical football match, with 22 players and a referee on the pitch, it's slightly better than even odds that two share a birthday.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored; numerical claims verified by direct computation; pending independent review.

questions.scenario: You flip a fair coin 100 times and write down the sequence.
questions.question: How likely is it that somewhere there's a run of at least 6 identical results in a row?
questions.explanation: Any particular stretch of six flips is unlikely to match, but a sequence of 100 flips contains about 95 overlapping stretches, each another chance. Work it through and a run of six or more heads or tails appears about 81% of the time. Long streaks are a normal feature of randomness, which is why made-up 'random' sequences that avoid them are easy to spot.
questions.intuitionTrap: We expect random sequences to alternate more than they really do.
questions.principle: Over many trials, rare-looking patterns become likely because there are many chances for them to occur.
questions.funFact: Teachers can often tell real coin-flip records from invented ones just by looking for long streaks.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored; numerical claims verified by direct computation; pending independent review.

questions.scenario: You give a standard 52-card deck a thorough random shuffle.
questions.question: Has that exact order of cards almost certainly existed before in history?
questions.explanation: The number of possible orders is 52 × 51 × 50 × … × 1, written 52!, which is about 8 × 10⁶⁷. That's an 8 followed by 67 zeros. Even if every person who ever lived had shuffled a deck every second since the Big Bang, they'd have produced only a vanishingly tiny fraction of the possible orders. A thoroughly shuffled deck is almost certainly a new arrangement.
questions.intuitionTrap: There are only 52 cards, so the number of arrangements feels limited.
questions.principle: The number of orderings of n items is n!, which grows faster than exponentially.
questions.funFact: 52! is comparable to the number of atoms that make up our entire galaxy, by some estimates.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored; numerical claims verified by direct computation; pending independent review.

questions.scenario: A fair coin has just landed heads six times in a row.
questions.question: On the next flip, how likely is tails?
questions.explanation: A fair coin has no memory. Each flip is independent, so the chance of tails is 50% whatever happened before. A run of six heads is unusual, about a 1-in-64 chance from the start, but once it has happened it has no influence on what comes next. The belief that tails is 'due' is called the gambler's fallacy.
questions.intuitionTrap: We expect randomness to 'even out' in the short run.
questions.principle: Independent events have no memory; past outcomes don't change future probabilities.
questions.funFact: At a Monte Carlo casino in 1913, black came up 26 times in a row at roulette, and gamblers lost fortunes betting on red.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored; numerical claims verified by direct computation; pending independent review.

questions.scenario: A patch of lily pads doubles in area every day. On day 30 it covers the whole pond.
questions.question: On which day did it cover half the pond?
questions.explanation: If the patch doubles every day and the pond is full on day 30, it must have been half full the day before. On day 25 it covered only about 3% of the pond, and an observer would have seen mostly open water five days before the end. Exponential growth looks harmless for a long time and then takes over abruptly.
questions.intuitionTrap: 'Half the area' sounds like it should come halfway through the time.
questions.principle: With constant doubling, going from half to full takes exactly one doubling period.
questions.funFact: This puzzle is a classic way of explaining why early warnings about exponential trends get ignored.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored; numerical claims verified by direct computation; pending independent review.

questions.scenario: A game show has three doors: one hides a car, two hide goats. You pick door 1. The host, who knows where the car is and always opens a goat door, opens door 3 to reveal a goat, then offers you a switch to door 2.
questions.question: Should you switch?
options: Yes, switching wins 2/3 of the time
No, stay with your first choice
questions.reveal: Yes: switching wins two times out of three.
questions.explanation: Your first pick is right only 1 time in 3, and nothing the host does changes that, because he can always open a goat door. So 2 times in 3 the car is behind one of the other two doors, and the host has just shown you which of those two it isn't. Switching collects that whole 2/3 chance. Picture 100 doors with the host opening 98 goats: switching becomes obvious.
questions.intuitionTrap: Two closed doors look symmetrical, so 50/50 feels unavoidable.
questions.principle: Information revealed by someone who knows the answer changes the probabilities.
questions.funFact: When Marilyn vos Savant published the correct answer in 1990, she received thousands of letters, many from PhDs, telling her she was wrong.
assumptions: The host always opens a goat door you didn't pick and always offers the switch
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored; numerical claims verified by direct computation; pending independent review.

questions.scenario: A sheet of paper is 0.1 mm thick. Imagine you could fold it in half 42 times.
questions.question: How thick would the folded stack be?
options: About as tall as a house
questions.reveal: Thicker than the distance to the Moon.
questions.explanation: Each fold doubles the thickness, so 42 folds multiply it by 2⁴², about 4.4 trillion. 0.1 mm × 4.4 trillion is roughly 440,000 km, more than the Moon's average distance of about 384,000 km. After just 10 folds it's only 10 cm; the explosion happens in the last few doublings, which is how exponential growth always behaves.
questions.intuitionTrap: We picture repeated doubling as steady, linear-feeling growth.
questions.principle: Repeated doubling grows as 2ⁿ: modest at first, then overwhelming.
questions.funFact: In practice paper resists past about 7 folds; the record of 12 folds needed a single sheet over a kilometre long.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored; numerical claims verified by direct computation; pending independent review.

questions.scenario: At the same price, you can have one 18-inch pizza or two 12-inch pizzas.
questions.question: Which gives you more pizza?
questions.explanation: A pizza's area grows with the square of its diameter, not in proportion to it. An 18-inch pizza has 18² = 324 'square units'; each 12-inch pizza has 144, so two of them have 288. The single big one gives about 12% more pizza, even though 2 × 12 = 24 inches sounds bigger than 18.
questions.intuitionTrap: We compare diameters instead of areas.
questions.principle: Area scales with the square of linear size.
questions.funFact: By the same logic, a 16-inch pizza has about four times as much as an 8-inch one, not twice.

questions.scenario: Consider the number 0.999… where the nines go on forever.
questions.question: Is it exactly equal to 1?
questions.explanation: One neat argument: 1/3 = 0.333… exactly, and three times that is 0.999…, while three times 1/3 is 1. Another: if two numbers are different, some number lies between them, but there's no decimal you could write between 0.999… and 1. The infinite string of nines isn't a process that 'never quite gets there'; it's simply another way of writing the number 1.
questions.intuitionTrap: We picture the nines as forever approaching 1 without arriving.
questions.principle: A recurring decimal denotes the limit of its sequence, and the limit of 0.9, 0.99, 0.999… is exactly 1.
questions.funFact: Every terminating decimal has a twin like this: 0.25 is also 0.24999…
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored; numerical claims verified by direct computation; pending independent review.

questions.scenario: A disease affects 1 in 1,000 people. A test catches 99% of real cases and wrongly flags 1% of healthy people. You test positive.
questions.question: Roughly how likely is it that you have the disease?
questions.explanation: Picture 100,000 people. About 100 have the disease, and the test catches 99 of them. Of the 99,900 healthy people, 1% get a false alarm: about 999. So roughly 1,098 people test positive, and only 99 of them are actually ill, about 9%. When a condition is rare, false positives from the huge healthy group swamp the true positives.
questions.intuitionTrap: '99% accurate' gets read as 'a positive result is 99% likely to be right'.
questions.principle: Bayes' theorem: the meaning of a positive result depends heavily on the base rate.
questions.funFact: That's why a positive screening result is usually followed by a second, different test.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored; numerical claims verified by direct computation; pending independent review.

questions.scenario: A rope is wrapped snugly around Earth's equator, about 40,000 km long. You add just 1 metre to its length and lift it evenly all the way round.
questions.question: How big is the gap between rope and ground?
questions.reveal: About 16 cm, enough for a cat to slip under.
questions.explanation: Circumference = 2π × radius, so adding 1 metre to the circumference adds 1/(2π) metres to the radius: about 16 cm. Remarkably, the answer doesn't depend on Earth's size at all. Do the same with a rope around a football and the gap is also about 16 cm.
questions.intuitionTrap: One metre spread over 40,000 km feels like it must be invisibly small.
questions.principle: For a circle, a change in circumference produces a change in radius of exactly that change divided by 2π.
questions.funFact: This puzzle has been in recreational maths books since at least the 1700s.

goDeeper.text: The original radius cancels completely, which is why the planet's size doesn't matter.

questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored; numerical claims verified by direct computation; pending independent review.

questions.scenario: You drive to a town at 60 km/h and drive back the same route at 40 km/h.
questions.question: What was your average speed for the whole round trip?
questions.explanation: Say the town is 120 km away. Going there takes 2 hours; coming back takes 3. That's 240 km in 5 hours, an average of 48 km/h. You spend more time at the slower speed, so the slow leg counts for more. Averaging the two speeds directly would only work if you spent equal time at each, not equal distance.
questions.intuitionTrap: Averaging the two numbers feels like the obvious move.
questions.principle: Average speed is total distance divided by total time; for equal distances, it's the harmonic mean of the speeds.
questions.funFact: If you drove there at 60 km/h, no return speed could make your round-trip average 120 km/h: you'd need to come back instantly.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored; numerical claims verified by direct computation; pending independent review.

questions.scenario: Hospital A has a higher survival rate than Hospital B for mild cases. It also has a higher survival rate for severe cases.
questions.question: Could Hospital B still have the higher survival rate overall?
questions.explanation: Suppose Hospital A takes most of the severe cases, which have lower survival everywhere, while B mostly treats mild ones. A does better within each group, but its overall average is dragged down by its tougher mix of patients, while B's average is lifted by its easier mix. Reversing a trend by combining groups is called Simpson's paradox, and it shows up in real medical and social data.
questions.intuitionTrap: If something is better in every part, it seems it must be better overall.
questions.principle: Aggregated rates depend on group sizes; a hidden variable can reverse a comparison (Simpson's paradox).
questions.funFact: A famous 1986 kidney-stone study found one treatment better for both small and large stones but worse overall.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored; numerical claims verified by direct computation; pending independent review.

questions.scenario: A share price rises 50% one month, then falls 50% the next.
questions.question: Compared with where it started, where is it now?
questions.explanation: Percentages compound on whatever the value currently is. Start at 100: up 50% gives 150. Down 50% of 150 is a fall of 75, leaving 75, which is 25% below the start. Losses hurt more than equal-sized gains help: after a 50% loss you need a 100% gain just to get back to even.
questions.intuitionTrap: Equal percentage changes up and down feel like they should cancel.
questions.principle: Successive percentage changes multiply: 1.5 × 0.5 = 0.75.
questions.funFact: This is why investment professionals talk about 'volatility drag': big swings lower long-run growth even when ups and downs are equal in size.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored; numerical claims verified by direct computation; pending independent review.

questions.scenario: Four cards each have a letter on one side and a number on the other. You see: A, K, 4, 7. Rule: 'If a card has a vowel on one side, it has an even number on the other.'
questions.question: Which cards must you turn over to check the rule?
questions.explanation: You need to look for cards that could break the rule. A must be checked: an odd number behind it would break it. The 7 must be checked too: a vowel behind it would break it. The 4 can't break the rule, because the rule says nothing about what's behind even numbers, and K is irrelevant. Most people pick the 4, looking to confirm the rule rather than to break it.
questions.intuitionTrap: We look for evidence that confirms a rule instead of evidence that could refute it.
questions.principle: A rule 'if P then Q' can only be broken by a case with P and not Q; test P and not-Q.
questions.funFact: In Peter Wason's 1966 experiments, fewer than one in ten people chose correctly.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored; numerical claims verified by direct computation; pending independent review.

questions.scenario: Before estimating what percentage of UN member countries are in Africa, people watch a wheel of fortune land on a number: 10 for some, 65 for others. Everyone knows the wheel is random.
questions.question: Does the random number affect their estimates?
options: Only for people who know nothing
questions.reveal: Yes: higher wheel numbers led to higher estimates.
questions.explanation: In Tversky and Kahneman's 1974 study, people who saw 10 gave a median estimate of 25%, while those who saw 65 gave a median of 45%, despite knowing the number was random. This is anchoring: an initial number pulls later estimates toward it, because people adjust from it insufficiently. It shows up in pricing, negotiations and even judges' sentencing.
questions.intuitionTrap: If you know a number is meaningless, you assume you can simply ignore it.
questions.principle: Anchoring: initial values bias subsequent numerical judgements, even when obviously irrelevant.
questions.funFact: In one experiment, the last two digits of people's social security numbers influenced how much they'd bid for wine and chocolates.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against the cited research; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: A sheet of white paper lies under a dim reading lamp indoors. A sheet of black paper lies outside in bright midday sun.
questions.question: Which sheet actually sends more light into your eyes?
questions.reveal: The black paper outside, by roughly ten times.
questions.explanation: Direct sunlight is hundreds of times brighter than typical indoor lighting. White paper reflects most of the light falling on it; black paper only a few per cent. A few per cent of sunlight still beats most of a dim lamp's light, roughly ten to one. Yet the black paper still looks black, because your brain judges lightness by comparing a surface with its surroundings, not by the raw amount of light.
questions.intuitionTrap: We assume 'white' means 'sends more light' in every situation.
questions.principle: Lightness constancy: the visual system estimates surface reflectance relative to the surrounding scene.
questions.funFact: The famous 'checker shadow' illusion uses the same mechanism to make two identical greys look completely different.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against the cited research; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: Each of your eyes has a blind spot where the optic nerve leaves the retina, with no light sensors at all. Close one eye and look around.
questions.question: Why don't you see a hole in your vision?
options: The spot is too tiny to matter
Your eye moves too fast to notice
questions.explanation: The blind spot is surprisingly big: about 5 degrees across, enough to make a coin at arm's length vanish, and you can find it with a dot on paper. With both eyes open, each eye covers the other's gap. But even with one eye closed you don't see a hole, because your brain fills the area with whatever pattern surrounds it. What you 'see' there is partly a construction.
questions.intuitionTrap: Vision feels like a camera recording everything faithfully.
questions.principle: Perception actively fills in missing information from context.
questions.funFact: Octopus eyes are wired the other way round and don't have this blind spot.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against the cited research; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: In classic experiments, people answer general-knowledge questions and say how certain they are of each answer.
questions.question: On answers people say they're virtually certain about, how often are they actually right?
questions.reveal: Noticeably less often than they expect.
questions.explanation: Studies of confidence consistently find overconfidence: answers people feel near-certain about are wrong more often than that certainty implies, sometimes in a sizeable minority of cases. Feeling sure is a feeling, produced by how easily an answer comes to mind, not a measurement of accuracy. That's exactly what this game's surprise rate measures.
questions.intuitionTrap: The strength of a feeling of certainty seems like evidence in itself.
questions.principle: Confidence and accuracy are only loosely linked; people tend to be overconfident on hard questions.
questions.funFact: Weather forecasters are among the best-calibrated experts: when they say 70% chance of rain, it rains about 70% of the time.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against the cited research; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: Right after a shocking news event, researchers record where people say they were and what they were doing. They ask the same people again years later.
questions.question: What do they typically find?
questions.reveal: The stories change, but confidence stays high.
questions.explanation: Vivid 'flashbulb' memories feel like photographs, but they drift like ordinary memories. When researchers compared accounts recorded the day after the 1986 Challenger disaster with accounts from years later, many had changed substantially, sometimes completely. Yet people were highly confident in their later versions, and some insisted their own original handwritten accounts must be wrong.
questions.intuitionTrap: Vividness and emotion feel like guarantees of accuracy.
questions.principle: Memory is reconstructive: each recall can alter it, while confidence can remain high.
questions.funFact: Studies after 9/11 found flashbulb memories decayed about as fast as everyday memories, but felt far more certain.
questions.source: Neisser & Harsch (1992); Talarico & Rubin (2003), Psychological Science
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against the cited research; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: Volunteers watch a short video and count passes between basketball players. Midway through, a person in a gorilla suit walks through the scene and thumps their chest.
questions.question: Roughly what share of viewers fail to notice the gorilla?
questions.explanation: In the original 1999 study, around half the counting viewers never saw the gorilla, even though it was on screen for several seconds. Attention acts like a spotlight: what falls outside it can go completely unnoticed, even when it's right in front of your eyes. It's called inattentional blindness, and it's one reason drivers can 'look but fail to see' a cyclist.
questions.intuitionTrap: We assume we'd obviously notice something so bizarre.
questions.principle: Inattentional blindness: unexpected objects often go unseen when attention is focused elsewhere.
questions.funFact: In a later study, many radiologists searching CT scans for lung nodules missed a gorilla image hidden in the scan.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against the cited research; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: You watch a video of someone's lips saying 'ga', but the soundtrack has been swapped for a recording of 'ba'.
questions.question: What do most people hear?
questions.explanation: Your brain doesn't process hearing and vision separately; it fuses them into one best guess about what was said. The sound 'ba' and the lip movement 'ga' conflict, and the brain often settles on 'da', a sound that fits both reasonably well. Strikingly, it keeps happening even when you know about the trick: close your eyes and you hear 'ba' again.
questions.intuitionTrap: Hearing feels like it comes purely from the ears.
questions.principle: Multisensory integration: the brain combines cues from different senses into a single perception.
questions.funFact: The effect was described by Harry McGurk and John MacDonald in 1976, after a technician mismatched sounds and lip movements by accident.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against the cited research; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: A full Moon rising just above the horizon looks enormous. Hours later, high in the sky, it looks much smaller. You photograph it both times with the same zoom.
questions.question: How do the two photos compare?
options: The horizon Moon is much bigger
The high Moon is much bigger
questions.reveal: About the same size; the horizon Moon is even slightly smaller.
questions.explanation: The Moon covers about half a degree of sky wherever it is. At the horizon it's actually about one Earth-radius farther from you than when overhead, so it's about 1.5% smaller in photos. The giant horizon Moon is created by your brain, probably because it judges the horizon as farther away and scales up its estimate of size to compensate. Nobody has a complete explanation even now.
questions.intuitionTrap: Something we can see so vividly feels like it must be real.
questions.principle: Perceived size depends on perceived distance and context, not just the image on the retina.
questions.funFact: Bend over and look at the rising Moon upside-down between your legs; many people find the illusion weakens.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against the cited research; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: You pinch your nose shut, pop a cherry-flavoured jellybean in your mouth and chew.
questions.question: What happens to its taste?
questions.reveal: It tastes only sweet; the cherry flavour vanishes.
questions.explanation: Your tongue detects only a handful of basic tastes, such as sweet, salty, sour, bitter and savoury. Most of what we call flavour is smell: aromas from food in your mouth travel up the back of your throat to your nose. Pinch your nose and that airflow stops, so you get just sweetness. Let go mid-chew and the cherry rushes back.
questions.intuitionTrap: Flavour feels like it happens on the tongue.
questions.principle: Flavour combines taste with retronasal smell; most food-specific flavour comes from smell.
questions.funFact: That's why food tastes bland when you have a blocked nose from a cold.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against the cited research; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: With your eyes closed, someone snaps their fingers off to your left, and you point straight at them.
questions.question: What does your brain mainly use to work out the direction?
questions.reveal: Tiny differences in timing and loudness between your two ears.
questions.explanation: A sound from the left reaches your left ear a fraction of a millisecond before your right, and slightly louder because your head shadows the right ear. Your brain detects timing differences of only tens of microseconds and turns them into a direction. The folds of your outer ear also reshape sounds slightly depending on whether they come from above or below.
questions.intuitionTrap: Locating a sound feels effortless, as if direction were simply part of the sound.
questions.principle: The brain computes direction from interaural time and level differences.
questions.funFact: Barn owls have one ear higher than the other, letting them pinpoint mice in total darkness in both direction and height.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against the cited research; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: You spin around quickly for 30 seconds, then stop suddenly.
questions.question: Why does the room seem to keep spinning?
options: Fluid in your inner ear keeps moving
questions.reveal: Fluid in your inner ear keeps moving.
questions.explanation: Your inner ear has three fluid-filled loops, the semicircular canals, that sense rotation. When you spin steadily, the fluid catches up and moves with you, so the sensation fades. When you stop, the fluid keeps swirling for a few seconds, bending tiny sensors as if you were turning the other way. Your brain believes the ear, and your eyes even flick to track a rotation that isn't happening.
questions.intuitionTrap: Dizziness feels like something in the head generally, not a specific sensor.
questions.principle: The semicircular canals detect rotation through the inertia of fluid relative to the head.
questions.funFact: Ballet dancers reduce dizziness by 'spotting', snapping their head round to keep their eyes fixed on one point.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against the cited research; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: You hold one hand in hot water and the other in cold water for a minute, then plunge both into the same bowl of lukewarm water.
questions.question: What do your hands feel?
options: One feels cold, one feels warm
questions.reveal: The 'hot' hand feels cold and the 'cold' hand feels warm.
questions.explanation: Your temperature sensors adapt: they report changes relative to what they've just become used to, more than absolute temperature. The hand adapted to hot water registers lukewarm as a drop, so it feels cool. The hand adapted to cold water registers it as a rise, so it feels warm. The same water feels like two different temperatures at once.
questions.intuitionTrap: We treat our sense of temperature as a reliable thermometer.
questions.principle: Sensory receptors adapt to steady stimulation and signal changes relative to that baseline.
questions.funFact: The philosopher John Locke described this experiment in 1690 to argue that heat and cold are partly in the mind.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against the cited research; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: You're watching for a light to turn on, ready to press a button the instant you see it.
questions.question: About how long does it take you to react?
questions.reveal: About a quarter of a second.
questions.explanation: Simple visual reaction time for an alert adult is typically around 0.2 to 0.25 seconds. Light must be converted to nerve signals in the retina, travel to the brain, be recognised, trigger a decision and then send a command down to your muscles. It feels instant, but at 100 km/h a car travels about 6–7 metres before the driver even begins to react.
questions.intuitionTrap: Our reactions feel instantaneous because we don't experience the delay.
questions.principle: Perception and action involve chains of neural processing that take measurable time.
questions.funFact: Reactions to sound are usually a few hundredths of a second faster than reactions to light.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against the cited research; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: You stare at a waterfall for a full minute, then shift your gaze to the motionless rocks beside it.
questions.question: What do the rocks appear to do?
questions.reveal: They seem to drift slowly upward.
questions.explanation: Some neurons in your visual system respond to downward motion, others to upward motion, and you perceive motion from the balance between them. Staring at the falling water tires out the 'downward' neurons. When you look at still rocks, the 'upward' neurons briefly win the tug-of-war, and stationary rocks appear to creep upward, even though they clearly aren't going anywhere.
questions.intuitionTrap: Motion seems to be something we directly see, not something the brain computes.
questions.principle: Motion aftereffect: adaptation of direction-selective neurons shifts perception the opposite way.
questions.funFact: It's sometimes called the waterfall illusion; Aristotle described something like it over 2,000 years ago.
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against the cited research; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: You throw a ball straight up. At the very top of its flight, for an instant, it isn't moving at all.
questions.question: At that instant, what is the ball's acceleration?
questions.explanation: Velocity and acceleration are different things. At the top, the ball's velocity is momentarily zero, but gravity never switches off, so the ball is still accelerating downward at about 9.8 m/s². That's exactly why it doesn't hover: an instant later its velocity points down. If its acceleration really were zero at the top, it would simply stay there in mid-air.
questions.intuitionTrap: Our brains blur 'not moving' together with 'nothing is changing'.
questions.principle: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity; in free flight, gravity supplies a constant downward acceleration.
questions.funFact: Passengers on 'zero-g' training flights float on the way up as well as on the way down: the plane is in free fall for the whole arc, not just the descent.
questions.source: Standard introductory physics (e.g. OpenStax University Physics)
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: A bird lands on a single bare high-voltage power line carrying thousands of volts, and sits there happily.
questions.question: Why doesn't it get electrocuted?
options: Both feet are at the same voltage
The current moves too fast to enter
questions.reveal: Both its feet are at (almost) the same voltage.
questions.explanation: Current flows through something only when there's a voltage difference across it. Both of the bird's feet grip the same wire a few centimetres apart, so they sit at nearly the same voltage, and that tiny difference pushes almost no current through the bird. The danger comes when a bird or a person touches two different wires, or a wire and something connected to the ground. Then a huge voltage appears across the body.
questions.intuitionTrap: We think of a 'live' wire as dangerous to touch at all, rather than dangerous to bridge.
questions.principle: Current flows only where there is a voltage difference; its size depends on that difference and the resistance.
questions.funFact: Large birds such as eagles are electrocuted surprisingly often because their wingspans can bridge two conductors, so power companies add wider spacing and covers on poles.
questions.source: Standard introductory physics (e.g. OpenStax University Physics)
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: You're sitting in a small rowing boat on a calm pond, holding a heavy rock. You drop the rock over the side and it sinks to the bottom.
questions.question: What happens to the water level of the pond?
questions.explanation: While the rock is in the boat, it pushes the boat deeper, displacing a volume of water that weighs as much as the rock. Rock is roughly two to three times denser than water, so that's two to three times the rock's own volume. Lying on the bottom, the rock displaces only its own volume. Less water is displaced overall, so the pond level drops, just a tiny bit.
questions.intuitionTrap: A splash and a sinking rock feel like they should push the water up.
questions.principle: A floating object displaces its own weight of water; a sunken object displaces only its own volume.
questions.funFact: The same idea explains why a steel ship floats: its hull spreads out so it can push aside a weight of water equal to its own.
questions.source: Standard introductory physics (e.g. OpenStax University Physics)
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: A car drives around a perfectly circular track. Its speedometer never moves from 60 km/h.
questions.question: Is the car accelerating?
questions.reveal: Yes, toward the centre of the circle.
questions.explanation: In physics, acceleration means any change in velocity, and velocity includes direction. Going around a circle, the car's direction changes every instant, so it is constantly accelerating toward the centre. That centripetal acceleration is supplied by friction between the tyres and the road. The outward lean passengers feel isn't an outward force on the car; it's their bodies trying to keep going straight while the car turns beneath them.
questions.intuitionTrap: We equate 'accelerating' with 'speeding up', and the outward lean feels like a real outward push.
questions.principle: Velocity is a vector; changing direction at constant speed requires an acceleration of v²/r toward the centre.
questions.funFact: On a curve of 50 m radius at 60 km/h, that centripetal acceleration is more than half of g.

goDeeper.text: At 16.7 m/s on a 50 m radius, a = 16.7²/50 ≈ 5.6 m/s², about 0.57 g. Double the speed and the required acceleration quadruples, which is why fast cornering demands so much grip.

questions.source: Standard introductory physics (e.g. OpenStax University Physics)
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: You take a bar magnet, with a north pole at one end and a south pole at the other, and cut it exactly in half.
questions.question: What do you end up with?
options: A north piece and a south piece
Two magnets, each with N and S
questions.reveal: Two smaller magnets, each with its own north and south pole.
questions.explanation: A bar magnet's magnetism comes from countless atomic-scale magnets, mostly electron spins, lined up together. Cut it anywhere and each piece still contains lined-up atomic magnets, so each gets its own north and south pole. Keep cutting down to single atoms and it's the same story. Nobody has ever found an isolated magnetic 'monopole', a lone north or south, although some theories suggest they could exist.
questions.intuitionTrap: The poles look like separate 'stuff' at each end that could be split apart.
questions.principle: Magnetic poles always come in north-south pairs; no isolated magnetic monopole has ever been observed.
questions.funFact: Physicists have hunted for magnetic monopoles in cosmic rays, Moon rocks and particle colliders, and have found none so far.
questions.source: Standard introductory physics (e.g. OpenStax University Physics)
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: You stand on a bathroom scale inside an elevator. The doors close and the elevator starts speeding up as it heads upward.
questions.question: While it's speeding up, what does the scale show?
questions.explanation: A scale measures how hard it pushes up on you. To accelerate you upward, the floor has to push harder than gravity pulls down; the extra push is what speeds you up. So the reading rises. Once the elevator reaches a steady speed, even while still climbing, the reading returns to normal: constant velocity needs no extra force. You feel acceleration, not motion.
questions.intuitionTrap: It's tempting to think 'going up' makes you heavier for the whole ride, but only the speeding-up part does.
questions.principle: Apparent weight = m(g + a): only acceleration changes what a scale reads.
questions.funFact: When the elevator slows to a stop at the top, the reading drops below normal for a moment. Briefly, you weigh less.

goDeeper.equation: N − mg = ma  →  N = m(g + a)
goDeeper.text: With a = 1 m/s² upward, a 70 kg person's scale reading rises from about 70 kg to about 77 kg.

questions.source: Standard introductory physics (e.g. OpenStax University Physics)
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: You're on a spaceship cruising at 90% of the speed of light. You point a flashlight toward the front of the ship and switch it on.
questions.question: How fast does the beam move away from you, as you measure it?
options: At the full speed of light
questions.reveal: At the full speed of light.
questions.explanation: Light in a vacuum travels at the same speed, c, for every observer moving at constant velocity, however fast they're going. You measure the beam leaving at c. Someone watching from a planet also measures that same beam at c, not 1.9c. What gives way instead is time and distance: the observers' clocks and rulers disagree in exactly the way needed to keep the speed of light the same for both. That single fact is the foundation of special relativity.
questions.intuitionTrap: Everyday speeds simply add up, like a ball thrown forward from a train, so we expect light's speed to add too.
questions.principle: The speed of light in a vacuum is the same for all observers in uniform motion.
questions.funFact: If a ship moving at 0.9c fires a probe forward at 0.9c, an observer on a planet clocks the probe at about 0.994c, not 1.8c.

goDeeper.text: Relativistic velocity addition. Put u′ = c and you get u = c for any v.

questions.source: Standard introductory physics (e.g. OpenStax University Physics)
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: A sealed, perfectly insulated box has gas in its left half and a vacuum in its right half, separated by a thin wall. You remove the wall and the gas rushes to fill the whole box.
questions.question: Once it settles, what has happened to the gas's temperature?
questions.explanation: Gases cool when they expand by pushing something, like a piston or the air outside a spray can, because they spend energy doing that work. Here the gas expands into empty space, so it pushes against nothing and does no work, and no heat can enter or leave. Its internal energy stays the same, and for an ideal gas internal energy depends only on temperature. So the temperature doesn't change, even though the pressure halves.
questions.intuitionTrap: We associate expanding gas with cooling, like the cold blast from a spray can.
questions.principle: For an ideal gas, internal energy depends only on temperature; a free expansion does no work and exchanges no heat.
questions.funFact: The process only runs one way: the gas never gathers itself back into one half. Its entropy has increased even though its energy hasn't changed.
questions.caveat: Real gases change temperature slightly in a free expansion, usually cooling, because their molecules attract each other a little.
assumptions: No heat enters or leaves the box
questions.source: Standard introductory physics (e.g. OpenStax University Physics)
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: Imagine a magical elevator that carries you 2,000 km straight down into the Earth, about a third of the way to the centre.
questions.question: Compared with standing on the surface, how much do you weigh down there?
questions.reveal: Roughly the same, in fact very slightly more.
questions.explanation: For a planet of uniform density, the answer would be 'less': only the mass beneath you pulls you down, and gravity falls steadily to zero at the centre. But Earth isn't uniform. Its iron core is very dense, so as you descend you leave some rock above you but get much closer to that concentrated mass. Seismic models of Earth's interior show gravity stays close to its surface value through the mantle, rising slightly, and peaks near 10.7 m/s² at the core–mantle boundary.
questions.intuitionTrap: The textbook result, gravity falling steadily with depth, only holds if density is the same everywhere.
questions.principle: Inside a spherically symmetric body only the mass at smaller radius pulls on you, so gravity with depth depends on how density is distributed.
questions.funFact: Gravity only starts falling steeply once you're inside the core, finally reaching zero at the very centre of the Earth.
questions.source: Dziewonski & Anderson (1981), Preliminary Reference Earth Model (PREM)
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: A radioactive sample has a half-life of one hour. You start with 1 gram of it.
questions.question: How much of the original material is left after two hours?
questions.explanation: A half-life doesn't mean 'half now, the other half next time'. It means that in each hour, half of whatever remains decays. After one hour 0.5 g is left; after the second hour, half of that, so 0.25 g. Each atom has a fixed chance of decaying per hour, with no memory of how long it has already waited, so the amount keeps halving and never quite reaches zero.
questions.intuitionTrap: 'Half-life' sounds like two halves make a whole, so two half-lives seem like they should finish the job.
questions.principle: Radioactive decay is exponential: each half-life removes half of what remains.
questions.funFact: Carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5,730 years, which lets archaeologists date once-living material up to roughly 50,000 years old.
questions.source: Standard introductory physics (e.g. OpenStax University Physics)
questions.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: You're underwater in a swimming pool while a friend standing on the edge shouts your name.
questions.question: Why is it so hard to hear them?
options: Most sound bounces off the surface
Sound is much slower in water
questions.reveal: Most of the sound bounces off the water's surface.
questions.explanation: Water is actually a superb carrier of sound: sound travels about four times faster in water than in air, and whale calls can cross hundreds of kilometres. The problem is the boundary. Air and water resist being vibrated very differently (their 'acoustic impedance' differs about 3,600-fold), so roughly 99.9% of the sound energy hitting the surface reflects back into the air. Only a tiny fraction makes it into the pool.
questions.intuitionTrap: Muffled sound suggests water absorbs it, and many people also assume sound is slower in water.
questions.principle: When sound meets a boundary between materials with very different acoustic impedance, most of its energy is reflected.
questions.funFact: Ultrasound scans use a gel between the probe and your skin for the same reason: without it, a thin layer of air would reflect almost all the sound.

questions.scenario: A small steel bearing heated to 200 °C is dropped onto a huge iron block at 40 °C. The block stores far more total thermal energy than the little bearing.
questions.question: Which way does heat flow?
options: From the bearing into the block
From the block into the bearing
questions.reveal: From the hot bearing into the big block.
questions.explanation: Heat flows from higher temperature to lower temperature, not from 'more energy' to 'less energy'. Temperature reflects how vigorously each particle jiggles; total thermal energy also depends on how much material there is. The block holds more energy overall simply because it's huge, but its particles jiggle less vigorously. Energy moves from the bearing into the block until both reach the same temperature, not the same energy.
questions.intuitionTrap: Confusing temperature (how intense) with heat content (how much).
questions.principle: Heat spontaneously flows from a hotter body to a colder one, whichever holds more total energy.
questions.funFact: A swimming pool at 25 °C holds vastly more thermal energy than a mug of boiling tea, yet if you pour the tea in, heat flows from the tea to the pool.
questions.source: Standard introductory physics (e.g. OpenStax University Physics)

questions.scenario: You stand in front of a flat bathroom mirror and can see yourself from the top of your head down to your waist. You walk backwards, away from the mirror.
questions.question: Do you see more of your body?
options: Yes, more of you fits in
questions.explanation: In a flat mirror, your image is as far behind the glass as you are in front of it. Step back and your image shrinks in your view, but the mirror shrinks in your view by exactly the same factor, because both are getting farther from your eye in proportion. So the fraction of your body that fits in the mirror never changes. That's why a flat mirror only needs to be half your height to show you head to toe, from any distance.
questions.intuitionTrap: Things look smaller from far away, so it seems more of you should fit in the frame.
questions.principle: In a flat mirror, the point that reflects your feet into your eyes is always halfway between them in height, wherever you stand.
questions.funFact: Most people predict the opposite even after a lifetime of mirrors. Check it with two sticky notes marking the top and bottom of what you can see.
assumptions: A flat mirror fixed on the wall, with you facing it squarely

questions.scenario: An astronaut on the Moon holds a hammer in one hand and a feather in the other, at the same height. She lets go of both at the same instant.
questions.question: Which hits the ground first?
questions.explanation: On Earth, air pushes back hard on a feather's big, light surface, so it drifts. The Moon has essentially no atmosphere, so gravity is the only force that matters. A heavier object does feel a stronger pull, but it also has proportionally more mass to get moving, and the two effects cancel exactly. Both speed up at about 1.6 m/s², so they hit the dust at the same moment.
questions.intuitionTrap: Everyday life on Earth is dominated by air resistance, so we learn that heavy things fall faster.
questions.principle: Without air resistance, gravitational acceleration does not depend on the falling object's mass.
questions.funFact: Apollo 15 commander David Scott did exactly this on live TV in 1971, using a falcon feather: a nod to his lunar module, Falcon.

goDeeper.text: The object's own mass m appears in both the gravitational force and its inertia, so it cancels. Every object at the same place falls with the same acceleration.

questions.scenario: A single bulb glows, connected to a battery. You connect a second identical bulb in parallel, on its own separate path across the same battery.
questions.question: What happens to the brightness of the first bulb?
questions.explanation: In parallel, each bulb has its own path straight across the battery, so each one gets the battery's full voltage. The first bulb's current, and so its brightness, barely changes. What does change is the total current drawn from the battery: it doubles, so the battery runs down about twice as fast. Wire the two bulbs in series instead, one after the other on a single path, and they share the voltage, so both glow dimmer.
questions.intuitionTrap: It feels like two bulbs must 'share' a fixed amount of electricity.
questions.principle: Components in parallel each receive the full source voltage; the source supplies the sum of their currents.
questions.funFact: That's why home sockets are wired in parallel: plugging in a toaster doesn't make the lamps across the room go dim.
questions.caveat: A real battery has some internal resistance, so drawing more current makes its voltage sag a little and both bulbs dim slightly.
questions.source: Standard introductory physics (e.g. OpenStax University Physics)

questions.scenario: A planet has exactly the same mass as Earth, but twice Earth's radius. You stand on its surface.
questions.question: How does your weight compare with your weight on Earth?
options: The same, as the mass is equal
questions.reveal: About a quarter of your Earth weight.
questions.explanation: Gravity weakens with the square of your distance from the planet's centre. Doubling the radius puts you twice as far from the centre, so the pull drops to (½)² = ¼. The planet's mass hasn't changed; you're just standing much farther from it. Such a planet would also be strangely fluffy: the same mass spread through eight times the volume, so one-eighth of Earth's density.
questions.intuitionTrap: If the mass is the same, it feels like gravity should be the same too.
questions.principle: Surface gravity g = GM/r² depends on mass and on the square of the distance from the centre.
questions.funFact: Saturn has about 95 times Earth's mass, yet gravity at its cloud tops is only about 7% stronger than on Earth, because its radius is about 9.5 times larger.
assumptions: The planet is roughly spherical with its mass distributed symmetrically

questions.scenario: A proton is made of three quarks held together by gluons. Physicists have measured the masses of those quarks.
questions.question: What fraction of the proton's mass do the three quarks' own masses account for?
questions.explanation: Add up the rest masses of the proton's two up quarks and one down quark and you get only about 1% of the proton's mass. The other 99% is energy: the intense energy of the gluon fields and of the quarks' furious motion inside the proton, which counts as mass through E = mc². So most of the mass of you, your desk and the Earth comes not from the quarks themselves but from the energy of the strong force binding them.
questions.intuitionTrap: We picture mass as the sum of the masses of the parts, as it is for everyday objects.
questions.principle: Mass is a form of energy (E = mc²); in a proton, most of it is the energy of the confined quarks and gluons.
questions.funFact: Electrons get their mass from the Higgs field, but they're so light they make up only about 0.05% of a hydrogen atom's mass.

questions.scenario: Light is fired at a barrier with two narrow slits, but so dimly that only one photon passes through at a time. Each photon makes a single dot on a screen behind.
questions.question: After thousands of photons, what pattern do the dots form?
options: Two bright bands, one per slit
A random, even spray of dots
questions.reveal: Interference stripes, built up one dot at a time.
questions.explanation: Each photon lands at one single spot, like a particle. But as the dots pile up, they build alternating bright and dark stripes, the interference pattern that waves passing through both slits produce. With only one photon in flight at a time there's nothing else for it to interfere with: each photon's probability wave passes through both slits and interferes with itself. Set up a detector to find out which slit each photon used, and the stripes disappear.
questions.intuitionTrap: Interference feels like something that needs many waves, or many photons, mixing together.
questions.principle: Quantum objects propagate as probability waves that can interfere with themselves, yet are detected as individual particles.
questions.funFact: The same experiment has been done with electrons, atoms and even molecules made of hundreds of atoms.
questions.source: Standard introductory physics (e.g. OpenStax University Physics)

questions.scenario: A figure skater is spinning slowly on the ice with her arms stretched wide. She pulls her arms in tight against her body.
questions.question: What happens to her spin?
questions.explanation: With very little friction from the ice, her angular momentum stays almost constant. Angular momentum depends on how fast she spins and how far her mass sits from the spin axis. Pulling her arms in moves mass closer to the axis, so she has to spin faster to keep the total the same. It isn't free energy: her muscles do work pulling her arms inward, and that work becomes extra spinning energy.
questions.intuitionTrap: We expect a change in speed to need a push from outside.
questions.principle: Angular momentum (L = Iω) is conserved when no external torque acts.
questions.funFact: A falling cat uses a related trick, tucking and extending its legs at different moments to turn itself over with zero total angular momentum.
questions.source: Standard introductory physics (e.g. OpenStax University Physics)

questions.scenario: Two boxes made of the same material, one heavy and one light, slide across the same floor. Both start at the same speed and gradually slow to a stop.
questions.question: Which slides farther?
questions.explanation: Friction does grow with weight: the heavier box is pressed into the floor harder, so friction pushes back on it harder. But the heavier box also has more mass to slow down. The two effects cancel, so both boxes decelerate at the same rate and stop in the same distance. It's the same cancellation that makes heavy and light objects fall together in a vacuum.
questions.intuitionTrap: Heavy things feel harder to stop, so it seems they should slide farther, or that friction should stop them sooner.
questions.principle: Sliding friction is proportional to the normal force, so the deceleration (μg) does not depend on mass.
questions.funFact: Engineers measure friction this way: tilt a ramp until a block just starts to slide, and the angle reveals the friction coefficient, whatever the block weighs.
assumptions: Simple sliding friction with the same coefficient for both boxes

goDeeper.text: Mass cancels; stopping distance depends only on starting speed and the friction coefficient.

questions.scenario: You're inside a spaceship coasting through deep space with its engines off, far from any planet. You crouch on the floor and push off hard with your legs, as if jumping.
questions.question: What happens next?
options: You rise, slow down and fall back
You glide to the ceiling at steady speed
questions.reveal: You glide to the ceiling at a steady speed.
questions.explanation: With the engines off, you and the ship are both in free fall, so nothing pulls you back toward the floor. When your legs push on the floor, the floor pushes back on you, and you drift toward the ceiling at a constant speed until you hit it. The ship gets a tiny nudge the other way, but it's so massive that its recoil is barely noticeable. To push off you don't need gravity, just something to push against.
questions.intuitionTrap: On Earth every jump ends with a fall, so we expect a return trip.
questions.principle: With no net external force, motion continues in a straight line at constant speed; every push comes with an equal and opposite push.
questions.funFact: Astronauts on the International Space Station move around exactly like this, gently pushing off the walls with their fingertips.
questions.caveat: If the engines were firing, the ship's acceleration would act like gravity and you would land back on the floor.
questions.source: Standard introductory physics (e.g. OpenStax University Physics)

questions.scenario: A heavy truck and a small car collide head-on.
questions.question: During the crash, which vehicle experiences the bigger force?
questions.reveal: Exactly the same force on each.
questions.explanation: Forces always come in pairs: if the truck pushes on the car, the car pushes back on the truck with a force of equal size in the opposite direction, at every instant of the crash. So why is the car wrecked? The same force has very different effects on different masses. The car, with far less mass, undergoes a much larger change in velocity, and its occupants feel much larger accelerations. Equal forces, unequal consequences.
questions.intuitionTrap: Because the car suffers far more damage, we assume it must have felt a bigger force.
questions.principle: Newton's third law: the forces two objects exert on each other are always equal in size and opposite in direction.
questions.funFact: The same is true when you jump: you push Earth down exactly as hard as it pushes you up, but Earth's acceleration is far too tiny to notice.
questions.source: Standard introductory physics (e.g. OpenStax University Physics)
